#653. Germany's Gen Z protests disrupted by violence on Saturday

Nationwide protests led by young people were largely peaceful throughout the day, but reports about looting and rioting in the evening, especially in Frankfurt, overshadowed the spirit of the demonstrations.

This is a round-up of events at the youth protests across Germany on October 31 and November 1, 2026.

The Gen Z protests in Germany were mostly peaceful throughout the day, with tens of thousands of people having participated across big and smaller cities.

The peaceful demonstrations were overshadowed by reports about violence in some cities like Frankfurt (see below).

Hesse's state interior minister said he suspects that about 100 left-wing extremists instigated the violence in Frankurt.

There were instances of disturbances in Cologne, Hamburg and Bremen, too.

Riots, looting and attacks on police broke out in several German cities after protests by tens of thousands of young people across the country demanding better schools, relief from rising living costs and greater social justice.

The demonstrations had been largely peaceful during the day.

But serious disturbances erupted in the evening in several places.

Clashes broke out in Cologne on Saturday, with about 200 people involved in disturbances near Cologne Cathedral.

Police officers were attacked on the square outside the famous cathedral, with bottles and bicycles hurled toward them.

In a nearby side street, a window was smashed by an electric scooter thrown during the unrest, police said.

According to regional broadcaster WDR, other groups besides Gen Z demonstrators were involved in riots.

Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was deeply saddening that peaceful protests were overshadowed by "extremists who had nothing but violence in mind."

While Gen Z protests across Germany were largely peaceful during the day, clashes were reported in several cities as night fell.

German police sealed off a major shopping street in central Frankfurt on Saturday night after rioters smashed shop windows, looted stores and attacked officers following a demonstration.

Police closed Die Zeil, one of Germany's busiest shopping streets, to incoming visitors and urged bystanders to leave the area.

"Anyone not involved who is still on the Zeil can leave. Access to the Zeil is no longer possible," Frankfurt police said in a post on X and in loudspeaker announcements.

Chaotic scenes unfolded along the shopping street, where dpa journalists witnessed people breaking into stores and stealing trainers and other goods.

A specialist firearms shop was also targeted, prompting several arrests, a police spokesman said.

Police also reported attacks on officers, including attacks involving incendiary devices.

The violence erupted after police broke up a demonstration organized as part of the nationwide "Gen Z regelt" (roughly meaning "Gen Z takes charge") protests.

A large contingent of officers was deployed around the Zeil, with authorities advising people to avoid the area or leave central Frankfurt.

The German protests on Saturday are a part of a wider trend that has seen members of Gen Z, born between 1997 and 2012, protest in several European nations.

The wave of protest was triggered by students seeking education reform in France, with the standoff erupting in violence and looting two weeks ago.

For our standalone story on protests in France today, click here.

After a day of youth protests in Germany, senior police union representative Andreas Rosskopf said that there was no widespread property damage "so far."

"The Gen Z protests have turned out to be very peaceful," Rosskopf told the daily Rhenische Post.

While confrontations were reported after the marches ended in multiple cities, the people driving the clashes were "individuals acting independently, some of whom were masked."

Rosskopf, who represents Germany's federal police, said security forces acted very decisively and forcefully when such response was appropriate.

"Security forces remain absolutely ready to prevent any further clashes in the late evening of overnight," he said.

German security forces reported minor violent incidents in several cites in the wake of the Gen Z demonstrations.

In Hamburg, protesters at the city's Steintor square pelted the police with fireworks . Police used "immediate force" to clear the area, including using a water cannon.

Several police officers were injured during a similar incident in Frankfurt, according to a state interior minister.

Police also used a water cannon in Cologne, where the march was halted and turned into a stationary rally after some protesters covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.

A police officers sustained light injuries in nearby Bonn during a confrontation with a group of protesters.

In Berlin, the authorities noted a rally separate from the official event organized by the Gen Z movement. Police initially reported "isolated instances of throwing eggs and bottles" from a crowd of around 500 people. The authorities later also reported "illegal burning of pyrotechnics" and said the crowd has grown to around 3,000 participants.

Several police officers were injured in a clash with a group of protesters following the Gen Z demonstration in Frankfurt, authorities said.

"One officers could be injured more seriously, but this will need some more looking into," said Hesse Interior Minister Roman Poseck.

"We assume there were about 100 attackers motivated by extreme leftist ideology," the state minister said.

"They have staged a massive attack against the police by throwing bottles, stones and fireworks."

Police responded with water cannons and have the situation in hand, he said

Thousands of young people took part in protests in 34 German cities on Saturday.

German Gen Z protesters called out rising living expenses, remilitarization of Germany, and declining education.

Some of the protesters also called for Germany's current chancellor, center-right Friedrich Merz, to step down.

The protests were held under the slogan Gen Z regelt (Gen Z sorts it).

Police were out in force after many politicians warned that Germany will not tolerate the kind of violence seen in France in mid-October.

Police reported incidents in which pepper spray and water cannon were used to keep crowds under control, with protesters setting off fireworks and lighting fires.

Most of the demonstrations ended peacefully.

But tensions remained high in some German cities with reports of several police officers injured.

In Germany's second-biggest city, Hamburg, police estimated 6,700 people taking part in the demonstration.

They reported some groups of black-clad protesters, some of whom also wore face masks, pulling apart construction site barriers and throwing them on the street. Some of the barriers were later set on fire.

Police said they pushed the crowd back and used pepper spray to break them apart. The fire was eventually put out.

Following an initial estimate of several hundred people attending the rally in central Berlin, police said that some 5,000 people were now gathered at the Brandenburg Gate. The organizers, "Gen Z regelt" (Gen Z sorts it) gave a much higher number, saying 10,000 people were in attendance.

One of the speakers in Berlin, Kaja Schwab, decried false promises made by politicians.

The youth is being told that "we will do well if we work hard enough." In reality, the life is getting unaffordable and the young are "forced into military service," she said, in reference to Germany's renewed recruitment drive.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Thousands of young people have joined the demonstrations in over 30 German cities, with police reporting largely peaceful protests.

Hundreds also gathered in Hamburg, Erfurt, Magdeburg, Dresden, Leipzig,  Nuremberg, and elsehwere.

Retailers in several city centers had boarded up shop windows, particularly along luxury shopping streets, fearing unrest. Some shops were already closed for the Reformation Day public holiday.

No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available. More than 182,100 people had expressed interest in attending the events online.

Police in Cologne called off the planned "Gen Z regelt" procession after some participants covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.

"The demonstration will continue as a stationary rally," a police spokeswoman told the DPA news agency. Participants would remain on the Rhine riverbank, she said, appealing for restraint.

Attendance remained below the 15,000 people registered for the demonstration. Based on advance registrations, Cologne's protest was expected to be the largest in North Rhine-Westphalia.

Police repeatedly stopped a youth protest march in Stuttgart, citing participants covering their faces and leaving the agreed route.

Officers also reported smoke devices and firecrackers before the procession began. "Be loud, but remain peaceful," a police spokeswoman urged in a video.

In other German cities, police reported a largely peaceful start to demonstrations. Authorities estimated included 2,500 participants in Freiburg, more than 1,500 in Frankfurt, 1,200 in Mainz, 1,000 in Munich and 650 in Berlin.

No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available.

Politicians must involve young people in decision-making or risk the youth turning away from political institutions, education researcher Nina Kolleck warned.

Their exclusion "creates the impression that there is a policy for the old, but not for the young," the University of Potsdam professor told Germany's RBB Inforadio.

Kolleck pointed to decades of underinvestment in schools and the disproportionate impact of climate change on younger generations.

She warned that populist parties could exploit the resulting political vacuum if young people's frustrations continued to go unanswered.

#652. Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists

Scientists have proposed a surprising new explanation for why the universe exists, and it centers on a mysterious particle that physicists have largely overlooked for decades. Their theory suggests this forgotten particle may have played a crucial role in shaping the early cosmos and allowing matter to survive after the Big Bang.

The research addresses one of the most fundamental mysteries in physics: why does the universe contain matter instead of nothing at all? Scientists believe matter and antimatter were produced in nearly equal amounts in the early universe. When these opposites encounter one another, they annihilate and release energy. If they had existed in perfectly equal quantities, virtually all matter could have disappeared, leaving no material to form stars, planets, or life.

Now, researchers from the University of Southampton and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur believe they may have found an important piece of the puzzle. Their explanation involves a little-understood relative of the neutrino, an extremely lightweight particle that rarely interacts with ordinary matter.

A Forgotten Particle With a Powerful Role in the Early Universe

The team focused on a type of particle known as a 'decoupled' heavy neutrino. Unlike ordinary neutrinos, this hypothetical heavier relative has generally been considered too weakly connected to other particles to significantly influence the universe.

However, the researchers found that its unusually long lifetime could have made it far more important than previously thought. According to their calculations, the particle may have survived long enough to temporarily dominate the universe's energy density as the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang.

That brief period of dominance could have altered how the early universe evolved, influencing the conditions that ultimately allowed matter to outnumber antimatter.

Dr. Rishav Roshan of the University of Southampton, an author of the study, explained:

"This decoupled heavy neutrino has long been dismissed as an irrelevant background detail in particle physics.

"However, it decays incredibly slowly. As the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang, the particle lived long enough that it temporarily took over the energy density of the universe and triggered a matter-dominated period."

The findings were published in Physical Review Letters, a scientific journal of the American Physical Society.

How a Heavy Neutrino Could Explain Why Matter Survived

Previous attempts to explain why matter prevailed over antimatter generally left out the decoupled heavy neutrino. Because it interacts so weakly with other particles, scientists assumed it would have little influence on the processes responsible for creating the imbalance.

The new research challenges that assumption. The team found that even a particle with extremely weak interactions could indirectly affect the conditions under which matter gained its crucial advantage.

This imbalance, known as matter and antimatter asymmetry, is essential to understanding our existence. For reasons physicists are still trying to explain, the early universe ended up with slightly more matter than antimatter. That small difference allowed some matter to remain after most particles and their antiparticles annihilated one another.

"The fact that we are here at all proves that an asymmetry between matter and antimatter occurred," added Dr. Roshan.

"The decoupled neutrino shifted the temperature in the early universe at which fundamental particles - like electrons and other leptons - interacted with their anti-particles with the help of Standard Model Higgs boson.

"This temperature acts like a switch that shapes how the matter-antimatter imbalance was built up."

The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle associated with the mechanism that gives many elementary particles their mass. In the researchers' proposed scenario, the heavy neutrino changed the temperature conditions governing important particle interactions involving the Higgs boson.

By shifting when these interactions occurred, the particle could have influenced how the imbalance between matter and antimatter developed. In other words, something long considered insignificant may have helped determine why the universe contains matter at all.

Ancient Gravitational Waves Could Reveal the Answer

The theory could also have important implications for understanding how the universe expanded in its earliest stages.

Study co-author Dr. Sudipta Show of the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said the findings suggest that the forgotten particle may have dramatically altered the expansion history of the young cosmos.

He added: "It offers us a new explanation for how matter won.

"The dramatic shift in the early expansion of the cosmos leaves distinct but detectable imprints of changes, for example on primordial gravitational waves.

"These gravitational wave signatures open up new avenues for us to unravel the evolution of the early universe after the Big Bang."

Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of space and time. Scientists believe processes in the extremely early universe may have generated primordial gravitational waves that carry information about conditions from that distant era.

According to the new theory, the temporary dominance of the heavy neutrino could have left recognizable signatures in those ancient signals. Detecting such patterns could eventually provide a way to investigate whether the proposed particle really influenced the universe's earliest evolution.

For now, the explanation remains theoretical. But it offers physicists a new possibility for solving one of cosmology's deepest mysteries: how matter survived when its encounter with antimatter could have left the universe almost entirely empty.

Materials provided by University of Southampton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Earth’s Mightiest Heroes (from different Earths, actually) are assembling again in December 2026.

Avengers: Doomsday's cast looks ridiculously stacked, and it’ll finally realize the dream of bringing together the Avengers, the Fantastic Four, and the X-Men (Fox’s original ones, that is) on the big screen. It’s a lot to absorb, and we don’t really know what's going on, but the trailers released so far are promising.

Anthony & Joe Russo (Captain America: The Winter Soldier & Civil War, Avengers: Infinity War & Endgame) are returning to direct, so that’s a good reason to be hyped even if the duo’s post-Marvel career hasn’t been the most exciting. Stephen McFeely (one of their two go-to scribes) is also back, and Michael Waldron (Loki) is helping out as well. It’s an all-star team for the most ambitious MCU project to date, at least until it all culminates in...

Release window: March 2027 | Showrunner: Dario Scardapane | Cast: Charlie Cox, Mike Colter, Finn Jones, Krysten Ritter

Daredevil: Born Again’s debut season was far from perfect, but most viewers agreed that Season 2 was a marked improvement.

Hopefully, that energy will continue in the third and final outing, as the Defenders reunite, with Finn Jones, Krysten Ritter, and Mike Colter all returning from their Netflix shows. Another shocker is the (unofficially) confirmed return of Elodie Yung’s Elektra.

We suspect some of these characters will be transferred to movies post-Secret Wars. In any case, Born Again’s final season should be packed, especially if Marvel Television is sticking to eight or nine episodes.

Release date: December 17, 2027 | Director: Anthony & Joe Russo | Cast: Chris Hemsworth, Chris Evans, Pedro Pascal, Robert Downey Jr.

Practically nothing about the follow-up to Avengers: Doomsday has been revealed yet (though we assume the MCU’s main players will be part of the ensemble), but we know it fully starts shooting in late 2026 and is eyeing a Christmas 2027 arrival. The plan is to leave a year-long wait between the two event movies, leaving fans hanging like back in the MCU’s glory days.

The title comes from Jonathan Hickman’s Secret Wars (2015), which is probably the main source of inspiration for the upcoming big-screen event. Incursions (realities bleeding into each other) have already been set up during the Multiverse Saga, and we know Doomsday directly deals with the multiverse’s breaking point, so it’s easy to see where the larger picture is going.

No spoilers here, but prepare for a very different kind of Avengers flick if Battleworld is indeed the main setting.

Release date: May 5, 2028 | Director: Jake Schreier | Cast: Kit Connor, Sadie Sink, Adam Driver, Christopher Abbott

Whatever happens in Secret Wars (we’ve heard Marvel Studios intends to soft-reboot), Phase Seven of the MCU will kick off with a long-awaited, fresh take on the X-Men — now part of the larger Marvel universe housing all characters. Thunderbolts* director Jake Schreier will be directing, with the same writing team from that movie joining him for another Marvel adventure.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day already did some heavy lifting when it came to setting up one of its leads (Sadie Sink’s Jean Grey), but it’s unclear how the whole group will be assembled.

We know for sure Cyclops (Kit Connor), Rogue (Inde Navarrette), Emma Frost (Samara Weaving), Storm (Maya Boyd), Angel (Asa Germann), Charles Xavier (Christopher Abbott), and Mr. Sinister (Adam Driver) are confirmed to appear, but the cast should grow in the coming months.

Release date: July 28, 2028 | Director: Shawn Levy | Cast: Ryan Gosling (more to be confirmed)

Phase Seven’s second movie will be an unexpected one, but the fan reaction to its reveal was glowing: Ghost Rider, starring Ryan Gosling, with Deadpool & Wolverine’s Shawn Levy directing.

The duo worked together on Star Wars: Starfighter, and it seems it went so well that Disney and Marvel are happy with them reviving the Spirit of Vengeance as the MCU expands its dark borders.

It’s too early to even know which Ghost Rider that Gosling will be playing (Johnny Blaze or Danny Ketch) or where the plot is going, but considering Levy’s past movies, we’re expecting an adventurous tone that blends well with Ghost Rider’s very striking, hellish visuals and darker themes.

Of course, this project is an invitation to add more magical beings to the MCU and explore the Strange-adjacent side of it. Maybe it’s our first step towards a Midnight Sons event movie? We can only hope.

Release date: December 15, 2028 | Director: Ryan Coogler | Cast: David Jonsson, Denzel Washington, Letitia Wright, Winston Duke

Ryan Coogler has taken a break from Marvel to make the excellent Sinners and help create a new iteration of The X-Files, but he’s confirmed to be coming back to wrap up his epic Black Panther trilogy. A while back, he confirmed he’d convinced Denzel Washington to join the MCU, and it sounds like those plans haven’t changed.

We also have a new T’Challa: David Jonsson (Alien: Romulus), who’s meant to play the son of the original T’Challa (Chadwick Boseman). If the years don’t make sense considering he was a kid in Wakanda Forever, wait until Secret Wars’ “soft reboot” for the answers.

What we know for sure is that series veterans Letitia Wright and Winston Duke are expected to stick around, but no plot details are available yet.

Release window: 2028 | Showrunner: Unconfirmed | Cast: Unconfirmed

Revealed at NYCC 2026, Zodiac is set to be Marvel Television’s next ongoing series after Daredevil: Born Again is over. Little is known about the premise at this point, though TV boss Brad Winderbaum has confirmed it’s a “globetrotting, international espionage show about secrets and lies and betrayals” with a packed cast of characters.

Word is the show is, more specifically, a British spy thriller with three leads, two male and one female. It’s expected to shoot in London during spring 2027, and chances are we’ll know much more about it well before that.

Of course, longtime Marvel TV fans are hoping for an Agents of SHIELD revival of sorts (its canonicity was never entirely clear), but it seems this show isn’t exactly that, though Clark Gregg (Agent Coulson) might be involved.

We’ve learned to never say never when it comes to Marvel comebacks, so stay tuned for more news.

Release windows: October 2027 / October 2028 / October 2029 | Showrunner: Bryan Andrews | Cast: Unconfirmed

Following a four-episode season in 2025, the animated series Marvel Zombies will be returning for three consecutive years (starting in 2027) just in time for Halloween.

The twist is that we’re now looking at three two-part specials: The Winter Soldier, The Fist of Khonshu, and The Last Guardian. It’s a huge departure from the previous plans with the Zombies and What If...? series, but it's one that could pay off.

Nothing is known about these small-scale projects at this point, but we know Marvel Zombies was a large enough hit on Disney+ to warrant more, and we’re okay with being surprised when it comes to format.

One has to assume these specials could work as one-shot comic books, but it’ll be interesting to see whether Marvel Television can tell cohesive and compelling stories with even shorter story arcs.

#649. NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past

NASA's Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have uncovered surprising clues about the earliest days of our solar system by examining some of the smallest and faintest objects ever observed beyond Neptune. The findings challenge expectations about how planets form and suggest that these distant, icy bodies have preserved evidence of their origins for billions of years.

For the first time, astronomers combined observations from Hubble and Webb to investigate trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs), tiny bodies that travel around the Sun far beyond Neptune's orbit. Researchers discovered 27 previously unknown objects, but their findings revealed an unexpected puzzle. There were fewer small objects than some theories predicted, and their colors closely resembled those of much larger objects in the same distant regions.

These frozen remnants offer a rare opportunity to study the materials that eventually became planets. Most are extraordinarily difficult to detect, shining more than 100 million times more faintly than objects visible to the naked eye. Two related studies published in The Astronomical Journal examined the newly identified objects to learn more about their sizes, compositions, and ancient history.

Ancient Building Blocks of the Solar System

Scientists believe planets began forming when tiny particles of dust and pebbles orbiting the young Sun gradually accumulated into larger bodies. Over time, these materials formed objects roughly the size of cities, known as "planetesimals." These early building blocks eventually combined to create the planets we see today.

However, that final stage of growth did not occur for many objects beyond Neptune. Instead of developing into full-sized planets, countless smaller bodies remained, preserving evidence of the solar system's earliest period of formation.

To investigate these distant survivors, research teams led by PhD candidates at the University of Victoria in Canada, working under the guidance of the National Research Council of Canada, and Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff conducted the deepest survey of trans-Neptunian objects to date. Both space telescopes observed the same region of sky simultaneously, with Hubble collecting visible light and Webb capturing infrared light.

By combining these observations, astronomers could examine the objects' colors, estimate their sizes, and determine how they orbit the Sun. Their colors are especially valuable because they provide clues about the chemical makeup of their surfaces, much like fingerprints that reveal an object's identity and history.

The researchers focused on two distinct populations of trans-Neptunian objects, known as dynamically "cold" and dynamically "hot" TNOs. These descriptions refer to their orbital behavior rather than their temperatures.

Cold objects have largely remained in the regions where they originally formed. They follow relatively circular paths around the Sun and stay close to the plane in which most of the solar system's planets orbit.

Hot objects have experienced a much more turbulent history. They originally formed between the present-day orbits of Uranus and Neptune but were scattered outward as the giant planets shifted positions early in the solar system's development. Their current orbits are much more elongated, and they travel above and below the solar system's main orbital plane.

Despite these dramatically different histories, the two populations revealed an unexpected similarity. Even the smallest objects appear to have retained surface characteristics resembling those of their larger counterparts.

Tiny Worlds Preserve Their Ancient Origins

Before the observations, scientists suspected that smaller TNOs would show clear evidence of repeated collisions over billions of years. Impacts could have fractured the objects and exposed fresh material, potentially changing their surface compositions and colors.

Instead, the newly discovered objects displayed the same general color relationships seen among larger TNOs. This suggests that collisions may have altered their surfaces much less than expected.

One possibility is that these objects have experienced fewer impacts than astronomers previously assumed. Another is that their surfaces somehow retain their original compositions even after collisions. Researchers have not yet determined which explanation is correct.

"You could imagine a scenario where getting knocked around and fragmented would change the surface composition, and then you would see a different surface color for tiny TNOs compared to their larger siblings. So it's really fascinating to see that the smallest objects are somehow 'remembering' and preserving the history of how they were made," said Northern Arizona University PhD candidate Anastasia Morgan, who led the study of color and composition.

"These dynamically 'hot' TNOs retain a signature of where they were born, even though they've been orbitally scrambled since then," said co-author David Trilling of Northern Arizona University.

The observations indicate that both hot and cold TNOs have maintained color patterns linked to their formation, with surprisingly little apparent change since the solar system's beginnings. These ancient objects may therefore preserve important information about the environments in which they first took shape.

Webb Finds Fewer Tiny Worlds Than Expected

The James Webb Space Telescope also provided another important piece of the puzzle. Its observations allowed scientists to examine how many objects exist at different sizes, revealing an unexpected resemblance between the two populations.

Although hot and cold TNOs formed in different parts of the early solar system, their overall size distributions were remarkably alike. This suggests that the processes responsible for creating planetesimals may have operated in much the same way across different environments.

"It's very interesting that the process of planetesimal formation ends up producing the same distribution of sizes for both cold and hot populations, despite forming in different regions of the early solar system. The process seems to be insensitive to disk conditions, producing similar planetesimal sizes whether the disk is hot or cold, and dense or fluffy," said University of Victoria PhD candidate Marielle Eduardo, who led the study on size distribution.

The researchers also identified a surprising shortage of very small TNOs compared with predictions from some existing planet formation models. Understanding why fewer objects were detected could help scientists refine their explanations of how the solar system's original building blocks developed.

Webb's extraordinary sensitivity made it possible to discover 27 exceptionally faint objects. One was so dim that detecting it would be comparable to standing on Earth and spotting a small swarm of fireflies on the Moon.

The smallest object measured just 3 miles (5 kilometers) across, making it approximately five times smaller than the objects detectable with even the most sensitive telescopes on the ground.

Hubble and Webb Reveal New Clues to Planet Formation

These discoveries depended on the complementary capabilities of NASA's two powerful space observatories. Hubble's ability to detect visible light and Webb's sensitivity to infrared light gave scientists a more complete picture of the distant objects than either telescope could have provided independently.

Together, the telescopes have opened a new window into a largely unexplored population of ancient solar system remnants. Their surprising similarities, preserved surface characteristics, and unexpected numbers offer important clues about the processes that shaped the planets billions of years ago.

Materials provided by NASA. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#648. ‘I Swear’ Star Robert Aramayo on the BAFTA N-Word Incident That Overshadowed the Movie and the ‘X-Men’ Wolverine Pitch He Keeps Hearing

Robert Aramayo is kicking back, eating a doughnut.

A red box of SK’s Donuts sits open on the table between us, lid flipped back, “Best Donuts in Los Angeles, Est. 1989” stamped across the top.

I joke with Aramayo before the mics are hot: This is why I booked the interview. I wanted some free food. He laughs, tears off a piece of a glazed and settles in as we sit outdoors on Variety’s rooftop. He’s four days into a Los Angeles trip for meetings, the kind of week where you shake a lot of hands. Nobody tells you what they’re for, and he’s doing it as the reigning BAFTA best actor victor for a movie most of America hasn’t gotten around to yet.

“I Swear,” Kirk Jones’ biographical drama about Scottish Tourette’s campaigner John Davidson, opened in the U.K. last October. It rolled into the 79th BAFTA Film Awards with five nominations and, on Feb. 22, handed the 33-year-old from Hull, East Yorkshire, both the Rising Star Award and leading actor over Timothée Chalamet, Leonardo DiCaprio, Ethan Hawke, Michael B. Jordan and Jesse Plemons. Four of those men, save for Plemons, were nominated at the Oscars. Nobody had ever won both in the same night. Sony Pictures Classics didn’t open the film stateside until April 24, which makes it eligible for this year’s Oscar lineup, where Aramayo faces a barrage of new leading contenders such as Andrew Scott, John Malkovich, Pedro Pascal, Matt Damon and more.

And as more viewers continue to discover “I Swear,” Aramayo could be a viable (and worthy) dark horse entrant to the Oscar conversation.

That split calendar is one reason the film plays like a new movie on a second look. The other reason is what happened on the BAFTA night itself. The real-life Davidson, attending as an executive producer on the film, sat near a live microphone, a few seats behind Aramayo. His involuntary vocal tics, including a racial slur, shouted as Jordan and Delroy Lindo presented. They were heard on the broadcast, and BAFTA apologized to the presenters. Davidson, who left the ceremony on his own in the second half, told Variety afterward he felt “a wave of shame.”

And for weeks, the discourse swallowed the film whole.

Aramayo isn’t sitting here to relitigate the controversy. He’s here to talk about the man he spent three months with before cameras rolled and now counts him and his family as close friends. When the BAFTA envelope opened and his name was called, Davidson was the first face he saw backstage afterward. “He was waiting for me, and we had this massive hug,” Aramayo recalls.

“Tourette’s is funny until it’s not,” someone told him during his research, and he keeps circling back to it. Some tics make a room laugh. Some tics hurt. “All those responses are human responses,” he tells Variety. “But at the same time, I see John and his experience and I know how difficult it is for him.”

What he wanted from the performance, and what he credits Jones for protecting, is a story about a person and not his diagnosis. “This isn’t a story about Tourette’s. It’s a story about John and all of the given circumstances that surround John.”

Aramayo is candid about the fear, as well as the script that scared him. We chuckle that Robert Downey Jr.’s Sean Penn speech in “Tropic Thunder” (2008) has scarred actors forever when taking on a disabled character.

But he felt safe because of the charities attached, Tourette Scotland and Tourette’s Action, which made him feel safer. Of course, Davidson’s blessing made him feel honored. But the truth is, none of it made him feel calm. He describes the night of his win in fragments: a blur when the name was read, a staircase and no idea what he was going to say. “There are honestly moments between them and me walking off the stage that I don’t remember.”

Between bites, we get to the rest, sit back and talk about the movie itself and the legends that surround it: Peter Mullan, whom he films alongside and whom once greeted with an improvised line that resulted in a “Wow, OK, this is a lot.” A third season of “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” is coming, which he calls darker, with Sauron out in the open.

He talks about Paul Thomas Anderson, the director he most wants to work with, whom he’s met and would still be terrified to work with.

And, because I can’t help myself, I pitch that Marvel Studios should keep his number for the day Hugh Jackman decides to hang up the claws on Wolverine and bring a new one into the MCU, especially with a new “X-Men” film on the horizon.

The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Where did you grow up, and how did you get into this crazy business?

I was always acting as a kid in Hull, in East Yorkshire, which is also where Tom Courtenay is from, so I’m very proud of that. I was part of Hull Truck Youth Theatre, which used to be a big touring company back in the day and has a really good youth theater. When I was 17, I decided I wanted to do something different. I didn’t want to go to a British drama school, so I applied to Juilliard and went there.

Do you get impostor syndrome? Has it sunk in that you’ve actually “made it?”

It’s not a conscious thing. It would be great if this industry worked like, you get this job, then you progress to that job and now you’re at that level. It just doesn’t work like that. In some ways, that’s brilliant, because you have to stay on your toes. I did my first play this year, and it was the most humbling experience. Theater training was all I did until I graduated, and then I just did film and TV. Being on the stage again, I was like, oh my word. Taking stuff for granted, thinking it’s going to be this way now, is so dangerous.

How did you hear about “I Swear,” and were you nervous to take it on?

The script and the story felt like a huge challenge. It was intimidating, and I was scared. But when I heard the movie was connected to Tourette Scotland and Tourettes Action, the big charities in the U.K., and that John was creating the story with Kirk, a lot of things made me feel better. It felt safe. But I was terrified.

Did you think this could be a career ender?

Did I consciously think that? No. Because very quickly, Kirk wanted to get me on a plane to Scotland to meet John and as soon as you sit down with that man, you’re like, “I’d just be honored to play him.” He was really passionate about it, and that helped.

How much did you know about Tourette’s before taking on the role, and what did you learn?

John is a good subject for a film about a person living with Tourette’s because when you see John’s tics, you think, “That’s what I understand Tourette’s to be.” But what I experienced in research was the social isolation of people whose tics aren’t as overt. There are tics you don’t see that you can’t recognize as a tic. And the chronic pain that goes along with repetitive motions can create big issues down the line. If somebody doesn’t understand what they’re seeing is Tourette’s, they think you’re just being weird. I met people who said part of them wishes they had coprolalia because it’s so identifiable as Tourette’s. And a tic coming out of a 12-year-old’s mouth versus a 55-year-old’s mouth, the same tic, is experienced differently by society. The education for me was enormous.

The scene where John puts on the device for the first time, walks into the library and comes back and asks, “Can I keep it?” On my second viewing, I felt the ache of seeing someone wanting to be seen as “normal” but also wrestling with betraying who you are. Did you see it like that?

I think it’s a natural response. The dialogue around the band is really interesting, and the way John feels about it is complex because it becomes part of who you are. It’s part of your identity. His first impulse would be, “Can I keep it? Can I always wear it?” But in time, he might find, “Is it another form of suppression? Is there a cost to that?” How people feel about it is their own. Somebody said something to me about Tourette’s that really resonates: “If you’ve met one person with Tourette’s, you’ve met one person with Tourette’s.”

My son has autism. When he was diagnosed, people unfamiliar with it would sometimes ask, from a place of love, “Is there a cure?” I’ve also been asked whether, if there were a cure, I’d want it for my son. I feel like that’s the same as asking if I want a different kid. I wonder if John feels the same way about himself. If you take Tourette’s away, John is still John, but you’re also taking away something that helped make him who he is.

It comes back to the film’s messaging. One of the first things I thought was, “This is a story about John Davidson’s life. This isn’t a story about Tourette’s. It’s a story about John and the circumstances surrounding him, the choices he makes and his wants and desires.” That’s why I like that the story is, in parts, very simple. We’re going in for a job interview; we all want the job. John wants to get the job. He’s got his own circumstances that are part of his life. That speaks to Kirk’s vision. He wanted an element of just someone living a life. If you spend time with people with Tourette’s, sometimes that is the event. Going to a fast-food restaurant and ordering quickly is easy for us. It’s not always the case.

What do you want people to know about the film that gets lost in translation, especially after BAFTA?

I hope people experience John’s story and then go and Google what Tourette’s is. The Tourette Association of America told me that one in 50 kids in America live with a persistent tic disorder, and one in 160 are living with Tourette’s. So it’s in schools. You can’t avoid it. Watch the documentaries about John; they’re fascinating. And maybe Google the TAA.

You spent three months with John before shooting. What was the first thing he said to you after you won the BAFTA?

He was there. The first person I saw was John. He was waiting for me, and we had this massive hug. He couldn’t believe it. Unbelievably supportive. I’m very close with him now and the whole family. I feel very lucky to have them in my life.

You were a BAFTA winner before the movie had even opened in the U.S. When they said your name, what went through your head?

It was massive. I’d just won the Rising Star Award, which I couldn’t believe and they had to take me from that and back to my seat. I was thinking, I’m going to have to do all this press now; I hope I say the right thing. I was not thinking at all about the other one. I thought I was sat there as a formality. Then when they said my name, I still can’t believe it. Total shock. Honestly, there are moments between then and walking off the stage that I don’t remember. I remember a blur when she read my name out, and then all of a sudden I was running down some stairs, with little fragments of thought: What the hell am I going to say?

Did you ever dream about winning an award as prestigious as BAFTA?

No. I really didn’t, because I remember growing up in Hull and seeing them on TV and thinking, wow, this is so special. And then all of a sudden you’re sat there with one. Unbelievable, and a really weird experience. Especially awards you’ve known about since you were little. It does weird things to your mind.

I wrote extensively about that night, trying to offer a perspective on both experiences in the room — from a father who has a son with a disability and a person of color who endures hurtful language. I also interviewed John Davidson himself. Were you disappointed that the media coverage afterward took away from what John set out to do?

I love the piece you wrote because it speaks to both experiences, and that’s really important. If John were here now, he might hit you [physically]. That will hurt you. It will also hurt John because he’s hit you. So I think what the film is trying to do — spreading awareness and education — is important. But the actual fallout and the people who were affected, it’s really unfortunate. It’s not a very nice moment. Somebody once told me, “Tourette’s is funny until it’s not.” That’s key.

There were a lot of tics that night, and some made people laugh, which is a natural response. Other tics, we know the story. Another thing people always say is, “Ignore the tics but not the person.” With John, I’ll always just let it go, let it go, let it go, whatever it is. Sometimes you can’t help but get hurt if he hits you or if the tic is hurtful verbally. Or it might even make you laugh.

All of those are human responses. At the same time, I see John’s experience and I know how difficult it is for him.

You were sitting a few rows from him. Did you want to run over and give him a hug?

Of course. I’m really close with John. At a certain point, John was just gone and I was just worried about him.

I read that you improvised a line to Peter Mullan that caught him off guard. How did you have that freedom?

They always encouraged every take to be different. That tic only happened once in that take, and a lot of that was going on with other actors too. Kirk is a really collaborative, open director who wants you to come with offerings. But I remember Pete being like, “Wow, OK, this is a lot.” I love Pete. He’s absolutely phenomenal. He loves the work and doesn’t take it too seriously, but once he’s in it, there’s no one you’d rather be in it with. I remember auditioning for a film years ago just because Pete was in it. What he’s done in his career is stunning.

You and Mullan are both in “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power.” Was “I Swear” easy because you already knew each other?

Not at all. I think I did one scene with him in Season 1. I was standing on a table; he was on a stool, and at some points, you’re not allowed to look each other in the eye. In this, we could properly work. Whether it’s loads of prosthetics and wigs or two people in a room, it’s the same job. That’s why he’s the best.

Do people stop you in airports and say “Elrond?” And what can you share about the next season of “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power?”

People do ask me about Elrond. It happens in airports as well; that’s the thing. I think it’s a darker season. Sauron’s out in the open, doing his thing. There’s paranoia in Middle-earth. And it was actually the shortest shoot so far.

What’s your favorite movie of all time, or the one that made you fall in love with movies?

“The Fellowship of the Ring” was a big thing when I was a kid. The epic adventure of it. It’s still my favorite of those films. But I also watched “There Will Be Blood” when I was quite young.

Who’s the director you want to work with the most?

What’s your favorite Paul Thomas Anderson movie?

Probably that, but I think “Punch-Drunk Love” is incredible. The score is fantastic. I’ve met him a few times, and I told him I’m obsessed. I don’t even know if I’d want to work with him because I’d be scared of letting him down. Every one of his films seems to have its own musicality. I don’t know how you create such eclectic films without giving in to the rhythm.

Do you worry about the business right now? AI, mergers, all of it.

I get scared. I’m constantly scared. But not in the classic sense of, “I don’t know if I’m ever going to get another job.” The ability to keep doing it is the biggest gift ever. Longevity. You look at actors who’ve been doing it so long, and the biggest gift is that they’ve been able to keep acting. So I worry about that. It’s a scary landscape all the time. I get quite overwhelmed.

What’s a role you’d most want to play if it got made, and would you ever consider doing a superhero movie?

Why don’t you answer the superhero part for me, and I’ll do the first part.

I mean … They’re building the “X-Men” universe. At some point, as talented as he is, Hugh Jackman can’t play that role forever. So when that Wolverine casting comes up, and I saw you walked in today, with the hair pretty grown out and big — I think I can see it.

I can’t even imagine. But you know what? You’re not the first person who’s said it, though.

Yeah, I mean, I’ve done them. I was in “Mindhunter,” and that was an incredible experience.

So you’re open to it? Before we drag this on any further, we want to make sure you would be.

I would be so scared. I absolutely love what he’s done with that role. And since we’re talking about “X-Men,” you’ve got to acknowledge Patrick Stewart. I was absolutely gutted. He’s one of those actors who was a big part of my childhood, like Harrison Ford. He did incredible work that so many different audiences watched. It’s so sad.

Just a small connection I noticed since you brought up Patrick Stewart. Christopher Abbott, who is playing Charles Xavier in the Marvel film, has the same PR representative as you. Is that a coincidence?

Oh shit! Oh my God. We do. You’re good! [Laughs.]

So, I’ll ask one more time then: is there anything you’d like to break here with Variety, exclusively?

I am working on something, but I can’t talk about it.

"The nation that leads in space will shape the future of humanity."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

President Trump issued a declaration yesterday (Nov. 3), proclaiming space open to all humanity for exploration, and the right of American citizens to develop and settle the solar system according to United States laws.

"The American Declaration of Freedom in Space," describes space as the "province of all humans" and asserts that the United States will lead humanity's expansion into the cosmos. The proclamation reiterates the administration's goals with NASA's Artemis program to return American astronauts to the moon by 2028 and eventually sending astronauts to Mars, but introduces no new funding, programs or policy directives.

"Our Nation will lead the way in the exploration, development, use, and settlement of these new frontiers — forging an interplanetary civilization founded on the enduring and inalienable rights of freedom and individual liberty," the document says.

Trump invoked America's "frontier spirit," highlighting Apollo 11 astronauts as the first people in history to walk on the moon's surface and robotic rovers exploring Mars as examples of U.S. leadership, and emphasized the country's flourishing commercial space sector helping ensure "American space superiority for all eternity."

"The nation that leads in space will shape the future of humanity," the declaration says, and pledges that America will carry the values of faith, freedom and individual liberty into an interplanetary civilization.

The proclamation also highlights the success of NASA's Artemis II mission in April, which carried four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon and set a record for the farthest humans have ever traveled from Earth. The follow-up to that mission, Artemis III, is scheduled to launch next summer (2027), and will test rendezvous and docking operations between NASA's Orion spacecraft and the program's two commercial lunar landers in low Earth orbit.

Artemis IV will be the program's first lunar landing mission, and is targeted for 2028. A December 2025 executive order from the President reaffirmed the goal of meeting that timeline, as well as the deployment of the initial elements for a permanent lunar outpost by 2030.

Trump's declaration yesterday does not establish new NASA programs, allocate additional funding or issue instructions to federal agencies. Its sweeping language, though, does echo some of the principles in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which guarantees freedom of exploration while prohibiting national sovereignty claims on other planets.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#646. Large Hadron Collider reveals evidence of Big Bang matter in surprisingly small collisions

The findings come one year after the first-ever oxygen collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). All four of the collider's major research collaborations, ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and LHCb, have now reported signs that this primordial form of matter can emerge when oxygen and neon nuclei collide.

The findings come one year after the first-ever oxygen collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). All four of the collider's major research collaborations, ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and LHCb, have now reported signs that this primordial form of matter can emerge when oxygen and neon nuclei collide.

The results challenge a long-standing assumption about the enormous forces needed to create such an extreme substance. They also offer scientists a new way to investigate the conditions that prevailed during the universe's earliest moments.

Quark–gluon plasma (QGP) is an unusual state of matter that appears under tremendous pressure and heat. At temperatures exceeding 100,000 times those at the Sun's center, particles such as protons and neutrons can no longer maintain their normal structure. Instead, they break apart into quarks and the gluons that ordinarily bind them together.

Physicists believe that this was the state of matter throughout the universe during the first millionths of a second after the Big Bang. Nearly 14 billion years later, researchers can briefly recreate these extraordinary conditions by smashing atomic nuclei together at extremely high energies inside the LHC.

For decades, scientists believed that generating this plasma required collisions involving very heavy atomic nuclei, particularly lead. Lead nuclei are more than 200 times heavier than the protons typically used in LHC experiments, making them capable of producing the intense conditions thought necessary for QGP to form.

However, recent discoveries have increasingly called that assumption into question.

Earlier this year, the ALICE collaboration, which specializes in studying quark–gluon plasma, identified another indication of QGP formation in proton–proton and proton–lead collisions. The previous year, LHC researchers had also reported the first hints of this plasma emerging from oxygen–oxygen collisions.

Now, more detailed investigations have revealed multiple signs that QGP can form in collisions involving both oxygen and neon nuclei, providing stronger evidence that the conditions required to create this primordial matter are not limited to heavy atomic collisions.

One of the clearest ways to identify quark–gluon plasma is to examine what happens when energetic quarks and gluons travel through it.

As these particles move through the extremely hot and dense material, they lose some of their energy. Scientists call this process parton energy loss, and it provides an important clue that QGP has formed.

The ATLAS collaboration clearly detected this effect by studying pairs of particle jets generated during oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions. These jets are concentrated streams of particles produced when energetic quarks and gluons emerge from a collision.

Researchers observed differences in energy between the paired jets, indicating that some of the particles had lost energy while traveling through the surrounding material.

The effect was especially pronounced during more direct, head-on (central) collisions. Such impacts are expected to create a larger volume of plasma, giving particles more material to travel through and causing greater energy loss.

Preliminary ATLAS results provide additional support for this interpretation. By examining charged particles that recoil in the opposite direction from photons, researchers found a similar relationship between energy loss and how centrally the nuclei collided.

The ALICE, CMS, and LHCb collaborations searched for the same underlying process using a different approach. Rather than focusing primarily on the energy of particle jets, they examined how the plasma appears to reduce the production of certain energetic particles.

CMS found that charged-particle production was suppressed in both oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions compared with proton–proton collisions. This reduction is consistent with particles losing energy inside quark–gluon plasma and provides further evidence that the exotic material can form in collisions involving lighter nuclei.

LHCb reported another important clue in a separate study. The collaboration investigated particles containing a charm quark and a lighter quark, comparing how strongly their production was suppressed in oxygen and neon collisions.

The suppression was more pronounced in the heavier neon collisions. That is precisely the kind of behavior scientists would expect if larger collisions produce greater volumes of plasma, causing particles to lose more energy as they pass through it.

However, reduced particle production does not necessarily prove that energy loss is responsible. Other physical processes could potentially produce similar effects.

To investigate this possibility, ALICE compared the production of neutral pions, another type of subatomic particle, in oxygen–oxygen and proton–oxygen collisions.

The comparison provided unambiguous evidence of parton energy loss in oxygen–oxygen collisions, strengthening the case that even relatively small nuclear collisions can generate conditions associated with quark–gluon plasma.

Researchers also looked for another distinctive signature of QGP involving particles made from a heavy quark and its corresponding antiquark.

These pairs can briefly bind together following high-energy collisions. Some are more tightly bound than others, making them differently susceptible to disruption by the surrounding plasma.

By examining which bound states are suppressed and by how much, physicists can gather additional evidence about whether QGP is present.

The CMS collaboration found evidence of this varying suppression in particles called upsilon mesons, which consist of a bottom quark paired with its antiquark. The researchers identified the effect by comparing oxygen–oxygen and neon–neon collisions.

LHCb also reported preliminary evidence of similar behavior, this time using data from proton–oxygen and oxygen–oxygen collisions.

Together, these observations add another piece to the growing body of evidence that primordial plasma can emerge in nuclear collisions much smaller than those traditionally used to study it.

The ALICE collaboration has identified yet another possible signature of quark–gluon plasma, this time involving the directions in which particles travel after a collision.

In preliminary findings, researchers observed that particles containing three quarks (baryons) showed a stronger preference for certain directions than particles composed of two quarks (mesons) during oxygen–oxygen collisions.

This behavior is known as anisotropic flow. Rather than spreading evenly in every direction, particles emerge in patterns influenced by the conditions inside the material created during the collision.

The leading explanation involves the formation of QGP. When particles with intermediate momenta emerge from this plasma, they can inherit collective motion from the quarks that make them up.

Because baryons contain three quarks while mesons contain only two, baryons can inherit more of this flow, producing the difference observed in the experiment.

This distinctive pattern provides another potential indication that the extreme matter of the early universe is being recreated in oxygen collisions.

Scientists are continuing to analyze data from collisions involving lighter atomic nuclei, searching for additional evidence of how quark–gluon plasma forms and behaves.

The findings are reshaping the understanding of the conditions needed to produce one of the most extreme states of matter known to physics. What once appeared to require collisions between massive nuclei can now be investigated through much smaller systems, giving researchers new opportunities to explore the behavior of matter under extraordinary conditions.

Meanwhile, CERN is upgrading the Large Hadron Collider into the more powerful High-Luminosity LHC. The enhanced accelerator will allow scientists to collect substantially more collision data and investigate the properties of quark–gluon plasma in greater detail.

With each new discovery, researchers are gaining a clearer picture of the remarkable state of matter that dominated the universe during its first fleeting moments after the Big Bang.

Materials provided by CERN. Original written by Rory Harris. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#645. Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience

After the Student List's election victory, Aleksandar Vucic's power apparatus is disintegrating. People want justice as soon as possible. But the losers still hold sway in the judiciary and administration.

Aleksandar Vucic is accustomed to the spotlight. As Serbia's all-powerful president, loyal media outlets followed his every move for years. His TikTok outbursts led the evening news. But on October 25 he lost the election to the Student List, and since then, a lot has changed.

Vucic complained at a press conference, before fewer microphones than usual, that the winners were practicing "revolutionary terror." He threatened: "If they continue to terrorize those who think differently – beatings, destruction and all the rest – and the state authorities do nothing, we will be forced to organize ourselves."

Vucic regards the immediate resignation of the general director of the Serbian state broadcaster RTS as an example of this "terror." Senior RTS editors have also been dismissed.

On Monday, a small group of protesters invaded the Informer TV station. Thousands of complaints have been lodged against Informer over the years for its demonization of Vucic critics. Now, journalists' associations are calling for its license to be revoked.

Tabloid media outlets loyal to Vucic have already changed their tone. Unlike Informer, they no longer refer to the Student List as "terrorists" and "mercenaries."

The List, which emerged from the student revolt, is made up of professors, activists and artists. In the election on October 25, it won 53% of the vote, leaving Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) trailing with just 39%.

Since then, things have moved fast. In many cities, citizens peacefully removed portraits of Vucic from municipal buildings. The public prosecutor's office for organized crime has launched investigations, including into electoral fraud. A special commission is examining the work of the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, which critics say did Vucic's bidding, and persecuted his opponents.

The accusations against him are old ones: that he and his system kept the media under tight control; that state contracts were only awarded to companies loyal to the regime; and that Vucic, his party, and the Serbian state had links to organized crime.

The catalyst for the revolt was the collapse, two years ago, of the concrete canopy on the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad. Sixteen people died. The accident is believed to have happened as a result of poor workmanship and corruption in the awarding and execution of the renovation contract.

Those who were celebrating in the streets a few days ago are already growing impatient. The new parliament has not yet been convened, and the SNS still controls many levers of power.

"A society that was oppressed for so long by a party that acted like a feudal lord now, understandably, expects justice," Dejan Bursac from the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory at Belgrade University told DW. "In this power vacuum, people are getting impatient."

Vucic and leading officials promise to be a strong opposition and expect to make a quick comeback once "this lot" have ruined the country. But the majority of critics are calling for Vucic to be investigated and charged. "The SNS people are acting as if they had lost a local election somewhere in democratic Scandinavia, not as if they were part of a deeply corrupt and criminal regime," said Bursac.

It's very common in Serbia for politicians to switch allegiance from one camp to another. They go where the power is. Even Vucic has admitted that many of his former comrades-in-arms are turning their backs on him. "We are going to see cases of people resigning or staying in the shadows, even putting themselves forward as informants for the next government," said Zlatko Minic from Transparency Serbia, an organization that monitors the work of governments.

The million-dollar question is: How much damage can the old government do to the new one? "There's still time for many officials to award contracts and create financial obligations for the agencies they run without necessarily committing a criminal offense," Minic warned.

However, those familiar with the situation said that for some time now the Student List has had contacts with officials in the police and administration opposed to Vucic's style of government. The winners of the election may now be able to prevent certain actions. On Wednesday, the List again demanded the resignations of leading officials in the police and judiciary. Whistleblowers were also asked to come forward if the outgoing government should try to "destroy documents."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In a symbolic move, Student List representatives held their first press conference in Pioneers Park in front of the parliament building. Vucic's followers fenced off the park in 2025, turning it into a pro-government encampment. According to investigative journalists, it also became a base for thugs and criminals who attacked anti-government demonstrators. The morning after the Student List's election win, its supporters went out with binbags and cleaned up the park.

The victorious Student List unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

"Our plan is to stabilize and develop the country, not to destabilize it with some abrupt change of course on foreign policy," Oliver Toskovic, a psychology professor and future member of parliament, told DW.

Toskovic said that, unlike under Vucic, the EU will not be misused as a "cover." Serbia's EU accession process recently stalled, with Vucic accusing "the West" of inciting a "color revolution" in Serbia.

"We are very dependent on Russia for energy. This is really a mistake of the previous government," Toskovic said. "But for that reason, sanctions right now would destabilize the country. And that would not be good for us or for the EU." How energy policy will develop under a Student List government is still unclear.

Where Vucic would frequently take aim at Kosovo, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading representatives of the new List have promised better relationships with Serbia's neighbors and a reduction in tensions. On Kosovo, Ilija Srdanovic, the Student List's lead candidate, has said the party is open to dialog with the government in the Kosovar capital, Pristina. He has already spoken by phone with the prime minister of Croatia.

The electoral process is not yet over. On Sunday, November 1, the vote will be repeated in some 50 polling stations because there were irregularities first time around. Once these votes are counted, parliament can be convened. The formation of a government is expected to be quick, but for now the names of the prospective members have not been disclosed.

This article has been translated from German.

#644. Over 20 Years, ‘Kung Fu Deadly’ Filmmakers Made a Supernatural Action Comedy That Blended ‘80s Favorites: ‘To Make it Coherent Felt Like a Really Fun Challenge’

Some genre movies are stripped-back exercises: lean, mean and to the point. Some films, like “Kung Fu Deadly,” take the opposite approach, dipping into multiple genres in a sumptuous visual feast.

“Deadly” follows Danny and Frank (Steven He and Michael Tient), two hapless exterminators in Dublin, as they are called upon to combat a supernatural evil. Audiences at genre festivals from Austin’s Fantastic Fest to Spain’s Sitges Film Festival have received it warmly, and it will have a wider distribution plan this spring. Related Stories 'Nobody Wants This' Season 3 Opens With 6.2 Million Views in Four Days ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ Creators Break Down Its Shocking Finale

Director Fergal Costello says he and cinematographer Shing-Fung Cheung thought about the visual style of this fantastical slacker tale as “primary color that’s covered in grime.”

“I just thought that was a visual language that reflected Danny’s journey,” the director says. “He has so much depth, color and heroism inside him — if he just believed in himself and wiped the grime off, wiped off the self-doubt. We wanted the movie to feel that, while being very colorful, because I frankly don’t think movies are colorful enough at the moment. Life is there and bursting out through the frame — you just have to look for it.”

Yet getting to that point of production was decades in the making. Writer Paddy McDonald says “Deadly” originally developed alongside fellow Irish writer Paul Markey and was born from their love of martial arts movies, from Shaw Brothers classics to Jackie Chan blockbusters.

“It’s been a bit of a labor of love for quite a long time,” McDonald says. “It was an idea I came across with him 20 years ago. It’s been bouncing around my life a little bit since then, but properly started developing it in 2011. I was living in Australia at the time. There’ve been a few different iterations of it and many, many drafts. I was living away from Ireland and moved back a couple of years ago and did a page one rewrite, bringing it back home. That’s when it started to make the most sense and had its original Irish voice.”

Once it came to filming, finding the right chemistry between the two central characters was central — and could help ground all of the disparate genres the film plays with.

“If we root the film in the relationship with the two boys together, Danny and Frank, then I think we can get away with all the other tones and not feel like they’re clashing together,” Costello says. “If we experience this clash happening through their eyes as they come into the movie and become more than just those lovable losers, the monsters and the magic and the comedy and the horror stuff will all work. Making the relationship between the two boys work was critical.”

Just as Danny and Frank found themselves trying to clean up supernatural entities, Costello and McDonald brought a parallel ethos to the set, where they mounted an eco-friendly production. In fact, it was Ireland’s first to be powered by green hydrogen fuel cells, versus diesel. It’s a milestone that the team is passionate about advocating for, as they can demonstrate the great results of environmentally friendly productions.

“While we were shooting there, we were able to power the entire thing with green hydrogen,” McDonald says. “The differences are how silent it is, how clean it is, how you can control these things. It’s like the difference between a diesel car and an electric car. You can turn it on remotely, you can turn it off remotely. There’s also data available to a production to understand the actual amount of energy that’s actually required. Once we got it set up and running, it was seamless. Whilst they’re a bit anxious about it at the beginning, I ended up loving it because it was so dependable, it was so quiet, it was so clean. It was a really positive experience.”

Much like taking the environmental challenge head-on, Costello says “Kung Fu Deadly” was a complex journey he couldn’t say no to.

“The idea of all those tones clashing together and trying to make it coherent felt like a really fun challenge, to be honest,” he says. “It wasn’t something I was very fearful of. It was something I wanted to jump at.”

Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The launch didn't according to plan.

For this mission, the Air Force was testing out the Super Strypi rocket. The rocket used a rail to help with the liftoff.

Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control. When it crashed, it destroyed all of the tiny satellites riding aboard the rocket. The cause? Likely a problem with the first stage motor.

The mission lost 13 tiny satellites known as cubesats. Cubesats are a popular option for space missions, because they are small and cheap, and they often operate in swarms. After failing to launch this batch of cubesats, the Super Strypi program never recovered from its failure, and the Air Force never tried launching another one.

The Super Strypi rocket was a 21st century take on a 1960s rocket. It was designed to be a modern version of the three-stage Strypi sounding rocket used for for reentry vehicle and anti-missile target tests. Its three stages, powered by Aerojet Rocketdyne solid rocket motors, was designed to reach orbit, rather than suborbital trajectories common to most sounding rockets.

The U.S. Air Force hoped Super Strypi would be a new tool for quick-response launches based on national security needs. Altogether, it was designed to launch small payloads of up to 300 kilograms into space for a mere $15 million per mission.

The rocket's primary payload was the ORS-4 satellite, short for Operationally Responsive Space 4, which was built for the Air Force by engineers at the University of Hawaii (who nicknamed it HiakaSat). It was designed to capture Earth imagery and monitor the environment over the course of a year.

The 12 other payloads on Super Strypi included eight cubesats for NASA's Edison Demonstration of Smallsat Networks mission, and as well as four others for universities that had been added as secondary payloads.

Since the Super Strypi failure, neither the Air Force or Space Force has opted to use the rocket for a new mission. The Space Force has turned instead to commercial companies for fast-turnaround launch support.

In June of this year, the U.S. Space Force teamed up with Rocket Lab to launch the Victus Haze mission with just 17 hours of notice, a new record to demonstrate short-turnaround launch response.
