#642. Scientists just found a loophole that could let black holes split in two

Black holes are known for merging when two of them collide, but could the reverse ever happen? Could a single black hole somehow divide into two smaller ones? A new theoretical study suggests that this extraordinary possibility may not be entirely ruled out by physics, although the conditions required would be extreme.

The research, published in Physical Review D under the title "When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies," examines the physical laws that keep black holes intact and whether certain circumstances could allow them to break apart.

"In our study, we investigate which physical laws normally prevent a black hole from splitting into two. We also investigate if certain circumstances may allow a split to happen," says Francesco Sannino, co-author of the study and a professor of physics at University of Naples Federico II in Italy and Quantum Field Theory Center at University of Southern Denmark.

The research team also included Giacomo Cacciapaglia, a researcher with the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) at the Laboratoire de Physique Théorique et Hautes Énergies, a joint CNRS and Sorbonne Université laboratory in Paris. Additional contributors were Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, both from the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark.

Why Black Holes Normally Cannot Split Apart

One of the biggest obstacles to a black hole splitting comes from thermodynamics, the branch of physics that governs how energy behaves and how physical systems change.

A central concept is entropy, which describes how many different microscopic arrangements a system can have while appearing unchanged from the outside. Black holes have entropy, and this property places important limits on what can happen to them.

For a black hole that is not rotating, dividing into two smaller black holes would reduce the total entropy. Such a decrease makes the process thermodynamically unfavorable, helping explain why black holes do not ordinarily break apart.

However, the researchers found that the situation could change dramatically when a black hole spins at an exceptionally high speed.

Extreme Rotation Could Allow Black Holes to Split

The team's calculations suggest that rapid rotation may create a narrow opening in the physical rules that normally prevent black holes from dividing. In principle, a sufficiently fast spinning black hole could overcome the usual thermodynamic restriction.

But there is another major obstacle. Even if a black hole could divide, the two resulting objects would need to move far enough apart to avoid immediately merging again.

"But the two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate," says Francesco Sannino.

The study's unusual title refers to the shape that a black hole's boundary would trace through space and time if such a split occurred. This boundary, called the horizon, would begin as a single structure before separating into two distinct branches.

Viewed across time, the resulting shape would resemble a pair of trousers, with one upper section dividing into two "legs." This is the idea behind the term "pair-of-pants topologies."

Extra Dimensions Offer Another Possibility

The researchers also investigated more unusual scenarios involving theories in which space has additional dimensions beyond the three we experience in everyday life.

Physicists have already identified objects resembling black holes in some of these theoretical models that can become unstable and start breaking apart. These possibilities suggest that the familiar rules governing black holes may not apply in the same way under more exotic conditions.

In certain cases, splitting could even become thermodynamically favorable, especially when one of the two resulting black holes is much smaller than the other.

However, a process being allowed or favored by thermodynamics does not necessarily mean it will happen. Researchers still need to determine whether such fragmentation can physically occur and what conditions would make it possible.

Could Astronomers Detect a Black Hole Splitting?

The scientists are now working to better understand how likely these events might be. The answer may depend on aspects of gravity that go beyond Einstein's theory, making the problem especially challenging.

"We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einstein's theory, and we are working to quantify this. We expect small primordial black holes to be more prone to splitting than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may detect a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT can search for signals from tiny black-hole fragments that might form during mergers," says Francesco Sannino.

Although there is currently no confirmed observation of a black hole splitting, the possibility of detecting signals from tiny fragments offers a potential way to investigate the idea. Such evidence could provide valuable clues about the behavior of gravity under some of the most extreme conditions in the universe.

Sannino is the director of the Quantum Field Theory Center (ℏQTC), which is affiliated with the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science (IMADA) at the University of Southern Denmark. He is also affiliated with the Danish Institute for Advanced Study and the Department of Physics "Ettore Pancini" at the University of Naples Federico II. In addition, he serves as a visiting professor at Durham University.

The spacewalk is scheduled to start at 8:30 a.m. ET.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Two spacewalking astronauts will finish upgrading the International Space Station's power system today (Nov. 5), and you can watch the action live.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and the Canadian Space Agency's Joshua Kutryk will install the eighth and final International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (iROSA) today, during a roughly seven-hour spacewalk that's scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT).

You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of NASA, beginning at 7 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT).

Today's extravehicular activity (EVA) will be the second in a week for Menon and Kutryk, who installed the station's seventh iROSA during an Oct. 29 spacewalk. That excursion was the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the ISS to date, and the first EVA for a Canadian astronaut since 2019.

Today's spacewalk will wrap up an ambitious ISS power upgrade that has taken more than five years to pull off.

"The installation job will complete the years-long process that began in June 2021 to augment the space station’s power generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts," NASA officials wrote about the EVA in a blog post on Tuesday (Nov. 3). That's a boost of about 30%.

Menon and Kutryk are currently sharing the ISS with five other astronauts — NASA's Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins and cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov.

Delaney, Kutryk, Teteryatnikov and Watkins arrived at the ISS on Oct. 1, on SpaceX's Crew-13 mission. Dubrov, Kikina and Menon got there in mid-July, aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

#640. Fox Commits to Carrying Non-Fox Content on Roku for at Least 3 Years as DOJ Closes Antitrust Investigation

The Department of Justice’s Antitrust Division Friday announced that it closed its investigation into Fox Corp.’s $22 billion acquisition of Roku after finding the deal “is not likely to result in harm to competition.”

However, Fox — which announced the completion of the Roku deal Friday — made several commitments to the DOJ in connection with the deal.

According to the DOJ, “Consistent with the Division’s finding that the transaction is unlikely to result in harm to competition, Fox has committed that Roku will remain an open and neutral content partner post-merger.” Related Stories 'Baywatch' Reboot Sets January Premiere Date on Fox

Specifically, Fox has committed to abide by the following four conditions:

The DOJ’s Antitrust Division opened an investigation into Fox’s proposed Roku acquisition, as is customary, and in September issued second requests for documentation to Fox and Roku. According to the agency, the division “analyzed whether the proposed merger may harm competition among free, ad-supported streaming providers” and “considered whether Fox might use its control of the Roku platform to disadvantage its content rivals post-merger.”

The Justice Department concluded that Fox’s Roku takeover would be “unlikely” to introduce “substantial risk of harm.”

“The Division concluded that the entry of free, ad-supported streaming providers would be timely, likely, and sufficient to make a substantial risk of harm to competition unlikely,” it said in its statement. “Additionally, the investigation found that, because Roku relies on a broad offering of content from many providers to attract consumers, the merged firm would suffer monetary and reputational harm if it attempted to use the Roku platform to harm Fox’s content rivals. If the merged firm were to degrade the Roku platform, consumers could switch to other connected TV platforms.”

The DOJ said the Antitrust Division will “continue to evaluate competition in the industry and may take appropriate action in light of changing facts or circumstances.”

It’s true that if Fox were to discriminate against TV and streaming rivals in deals for the Roku platform, that would hurt Roku’s existing business. In the first nine months of 2026, Roku has topped financial forecasts, delivering 23% revenue growth for the period to hit $4.1 billion in sales. About 49% of that came from advertising and 40% is from subscriptions.

Fox Corp. has consistently promised to continue to run Roku as an “open ecosystem” following the merger since it announced the agreement in June 2026.

“Beginning today, our top priority for the combined company is to continue to relentlessly serve audiences and partners, while reinforcing the openness and choice that is the essence of the Roku platform,” Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch said in a statement Friday.

Roku founder and CEO Anthony Wood is joining Fox Corp. as co-chair alongside Paul Cheesbrough of Fox Digital Platforms, a newly formed division housing Roku, Tubi, Fox One, Red Seat Ventures and other digital businesses. With the completion of Fox’s Roku acquisition, several execs are departing, including Roku Media president Charlie Collier and Tubi CEO Anjali Sud.

#639. IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos

An enormous number of invisible particles are constantly traveling through Earth, passing through our bodies and continuing into space as though almost nothing stands in their way. Known as neutrinos, these mysterious particles are among the most difficult objects in the universe to detect. Yet scientists are finding ways to capture evidence of their passage, opening new opportunities to investigate the cosmos and its most extreme environments.

Neutrino research has played a remarkable role in modern physics. Discoveries involving these particles have contributed to five Nobel Prizes in Physics. This year, physicist Francis Halzen received the prestigious award "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin."

George Fuller, a Distinguished Professor of Physics at the University of California San Diego, has studied nuclear physics, particle astrophysics, and cosmology for decades. He also collaborated with Halzen on an early scientific paper about IceCube. His expertise helps explain what makes neutrinos so unusual and why scientists built an enormous observatory deep within the Antarctic ice to study them.

Neutrinos belong to a group known as elementary particles, which scientists believe have no smaller components. They come in three varieties, called electron, muon, and tau neutrinos. Unlike electrically charged particles, neutrinos have no electric charge. They do have mass, but it is extraordinarily small, potentially around 10 million times less than the mass of an electron. Their exact masses remain unknown, as does the mechanism responsible for producing them.

Another remarkable characteristic is their ability to travel through matter with almost no resistance. Because neutrinos interact so rarely with other particles, they can cross vast distances at speeds approaching the speed of light.

Neutrinos originate from many different places, including the Sun, distant regions of space, and sources scientists have yet to identify. They are also astonishingly abundant. Estimates suggest the universe contains roughly 1089 neutrinos, equivalent to approximately one billion for every atom in existence.

"Neutrinos are truly ghost-like particles," stated Fuller. "It's hard to stop them. It's hard to catch them. How do we even know they exist or where they are?"

Ghost Particles That Pass Through Almost Anything

Despite their elusive nature, neutrinos occasionally interact with matter through a fundamental force known as the weak interaction. This force is approximately 20 orders of magnitude weaker than electromagnetism. Such interactions can cause neutrinos to scatter or be absorbed, providing scientists with a way to detect them. However, these events are so uncommon that observing them requires exceptionally sensitive equipment.

Their ability to move through dense material also makes neutrinos valuable messengers from otherwise inaccessible regions of the universe. They can escape from environments surrounding collapsing stars and black holes, carrying information that other forms of radiation might not reveal.

The scale of this invisible activity is staggering. Approximately 100 billion neutrinos pass through every square centimeter of your body each second, almost entirely unnoticed.

"Because the interaction is so weak, neutrinos can get through almost anything," said Fuller. "Light years of lead -- depending on their energy, they would go right through it."

How Scientists Learned to Detect Neutrinos

The search for neutrinos began long before technology existed to observe them. During the 1930s, physicist Wolfgang Pauli proposed that an unknown particle might explain why energy appeared to be missing during certain forms of radioactive decay. He initially used a different name for the hypothetical particle (he called them "neutrons" at the time).

Pauli understood how difficult it would be to verify his idea. He famously acknowledged the problem by saying, "I have done a terrible thing, I have postulated a particle that cannot be detected."

For decades, neutrinos remained beyond the reach of experiments. That changed in 1956, when physicists Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines successfully detected them in an experiment known as "Project Poltergeist."

The breakthrough established that neutrinos were real, but detecting them remained an enormous challenge. Scientists needed increasingly sophisticated instruments to investigate the rarest and most energetic neutrinos arriving from space.

Why Antarctica Is Ideal for Hunting Cosmic Neutrinos

During the 1990s, Halzen recognized that the South Pole offered an extraordinary natural environment for neutrino research. Far below Antarctica's surface, immense volumes of ice are exceptionally clear, with relatively few bubbles or contaminants to interfere with the detection of faint flashes of light.

His vision eventually led to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a gigantic scientific instrument embedded within roughly one cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice. To construct it, researchers drilled deep holes and lowered long strings of sensitive light detectors called photomultiplier tubes.

These instruments search for brief flashes of blue light produced through a phenomenon called Cherenkov radiation. The light appears when a neutrino interacts with matter in the ice and produces a charged particle traveling faster than light can move through that material.

By recording these flashes, researchers can identify evidence of neutrinos that would otherwise pass through Earth without leaving a detectable trace.

IceCube is particularly important for studying neutrinos that arrive from distant cosmic sources with extraordinarily high energies. Unlike the enormous quantities of relatively low-energy neutrinos produced by the Sun, these powerful cosmic visitors are extremely rare. The observatory detects only a few dozen of the most energetic examples each year.

When one of these neutrinos interacts with the ice, it can produce a rapidly moving electron or muon. A muon, for example, generates a cone of Cherenkov light as it travels through the ice. Scientists analyze the resulting pattern of light to estimate the neutrino's energy and reconstruct the direction from which it arrived.

For Fuller, these exceptionally energetic neutrinos are among IceCube's most exciting discoveries because their origins and the physical processes responsible for accelerating them remain poorly understood.

"Some ultra-high-energy neutrinos detected at IceCube have roughly 10 billion times the energy of a typical neutrino from the Sun. One detected by a similar experiment has an energy 200 times higher than that. We don't really know where that neutrino came from," he stated. "The fact that it got here at all may be saying something profound about the universe. In that sense, Halzen really is at the frontier of experimental fundamental particle physics."

Neutrinos Could Reveal Secrets of the Big Bang

The scientific effort to understand neutrinos extends far beyond Antarctica. Researchers at UC San Diego are also involved in another major observatory that could offer new insights into these elusive particles and the universe's earliest history.

Located high in Chile's Atacama Desert, the Simons Observatory is gathering information about the cosmic microwave background, the ancient radiation left over from the early universe. Often described as the oldest light in the cosmos, this radiation provides a valuable record of conditions that existed shortly after the Big Bang.

UC San Diego helped establish the observatory, and Brian Keating, a Distinguished Professor of Physics at the university, serves as its principal investigator.

Although the observatory primarily studies ancient light, its measurements can also reveal information about neutrinos from the earliest stages of cosmic history. The project could provide an enormous amount of new data related to these ancient particles, potentially offering insights that other experiments cannot obtain.

Fuller believes the anticipated observations could improve scientists' understanding of the Big Bang, the early evolution of the universe, and other fundamental questions about how the cosmos developed.

"Halzen's work, and the work of those he inspired with his vision, was foundational in giving humanity a new window on the universe and on the mysterious and notoriously slippery neutrino," he stated.

Materials provided by University of California - San Diego. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#637. Medicinal plants, lessons from mushrooms and the power of smell: Books in brief

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). Andrew Robinson is a writer based in London and author of Earthshock (1993), The Story of Measurement (2007) and Einstein in Oxford (2024).

Margaret Willes Bodleian Library Publishing (2026)

According to ancient Greek medical authority Hippocrates, “Nature itself is the best physician” — hence the title of writer Margaret Willes’s appealing book. Introduced with a substantial essay on European herbalism from medieval times to the present, it discusses 100 plants with medical properties, from alecost (Tanacetum balsamita, a member of the daisy family) to the yew tree (Taxus baccata). Each is illustrated with an exquisite colour drawing taken from John Gerard’s 1597 The Herball, or Generall Historie of Plantes.

When motor cars were invented in the late nineteenth century, their emissions were welcome at first, because they replaced the odour of horse dung that had reduced many city streets to “a state of organic olfactory crisis”, notes historian William Tullett. His engrossing history of smell ranges from ancient Christian aromas, through medieval Indian perfume and the scents of eighteenth-century slavery to the status of odour in twentieth-century China. It features “the foul, the fragrant, and everything in between”.

Jim Al-Khalili Princeton Univ. Press (2026)

Just before his death, Albert Einstein stated: “the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion”. In this compelling, if intellectually demanding, book about the physics of time, physicist and broadcaster Jim Al-Khalili disagrees. He argues that “the irreversible passage of time needs to be incorporated into the laws of physics”. By comparing the concepts of time in quantum mechanics, the general theory of relativity and thermodynamics, he concludes that time’s arrow is real, and makes the Universe tick.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03595-x

The Chinese roadmap includes an uncrewed lunar landing in 2028.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

China has given us some details about the epic moon landing it plans to pull off a few years from now.

Chinese officials laid out the roadmap for its crewed lunar campaign at the 7th Manned Space Symposium, which was held Oct. 31 and Nov. 1 in Beijing. The campaign consists of four missions, culminating in a crewed touchdown "before 2030," according to media reports.

That timeline — which is consistent with previous statements made by the China Manned Space Agency — keeps the pressure on the U.S., which aims to put its own astronauts down on the moon in 2028, via NASA's Artemis program.

Leaked slide confirms the four-mission progression toward China’s crewed lunar landing: 🚀2027: Maiden flight of Long March 10A carrying Mengzhou CSS cargo resupply mission, to validate the new human-rated vehicle and Mengzhou’s orbital operations in LEO. 🚀2028: First flight of the heavier CZ-10 with an uncrewed Lanyue lander performing a lunar descent and ascent test, exercising the lander’s propulsion and guidance. 🚀🚀2029: Dual CZ-10 launches of Mengzhou and Lanyue for a full-scale lunar-orbit rehearsal, demonstrating rendezvous, docking, and integrated operations. 🚀🚀Before the end of 2030: Dual CZ-10 crewed lunar landing mission.November 1, 2026

The first mission in China's four-part lunar campaign is scheduled to fly in 2027, according to CNSpaceflight, an X account that keeps a close eye on China's activities in space. The outlet cited an X user who shared a presentation slide of the plan.

That launch — the first of of China's new Long March 10A rocket — will send an uncrewed Mengzhou spacecraft to low Earth orbit (LEO) for a series of tests. Mengzhou, whose name means "Dream Vessel," is the next-gen crew capsule that will carry Chinese astronauts to lunar orbit.

Mission number two, launching in 2028, will involve a different set of hardware — the more powerful Long March 10 rocket and the Lanyue ("Embracing the Moon") lunar lander. This will also be an uncrewed flight, and it will mark the debut of the Long March 10, which will send Lanyue to orbit around the moon. If all goes to plan, Lanyue will touch down on the moon and then launch itself back to lunar orbit.

Mission number three, flying in 2029, will also target an uncrewed lunar landing, but it will feature two Long March 10 launches — one apiece for Mengzhou and Lanyue. The two spacecraft will conduct a rendezvous and docking rehearsal in lunar orbit, then separate for Lanyue's trip down to the surface.

This will set the stage for mission four — the real deal, in which two Long March 10s launch a crewed Mengzhou and an uncrewed Lanyue "before 2030." The two vessels will dock in lunar orbit, and the astronauts will move into Lanyue for their historic lunar landing.

Three astronauts will apparently launch on Mengzhou, and two of them will land on the moon aboard Lanyue, according to CNSpaceflight. The duo will spend three days on the lunar surface, conducting moonwalks on each of those days.

And about that "before 2030" timeline: The wording may have been chosen very carefully.

"One reading is that 2029 coincides with the 80th anniversary of the current government, creating a strong internal incentive to achieve the landing that year. At the same time, the technical schedule (new Long March 10 family, Mengzhou, Lanyue, dual-launch operations) remains aggressive; committing publicly to 2029 would create significant political exposure if any major test slips," CNSpaceflight wrote in a Nov. 2 X post.

"Using 'before 2030' therefore functions as deliberate wording flexibility: a 2029 landing can still be presented as an early historic success, while a slip into 2030 remains inside the stated goal without requiring a formal target revision. You just need to put 'year-end' after 'before 2030,'" the outlet added.

NASA's Artemis program has already sent astronauts around the moon, doing so this past April on the Artemis II mission. The agency is currently gearing up for Artemis III, a crewed flight to LEO that will test rendezvous and docking procedures between NASA's Orion capsule and one or both of the Artemis program's two private crewed landers — SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon.

Artemis III is currently on track to fly in the summer of 2027, NASA officials have said. But an on-time liftoff is far from guaranteed, as both Starship and Blue Moon still have some boxes to check.

Starship just reached Earth orbit for the first time on Sept. 28, for example, and it has yet to demonstrate off-Earth refueling, which will be a crucial part of any Starship mission beyond Earth orbit. And Blue Moon has yet to leave the ground at all. The Blue Origin lander is scheduled to fly for the first time next spring, on an uncrewed test mission that will send it to the lunar surface.

If all goes well on Artemis III, NASA will be clear to start prepping for Artemis IV, which will put astronauts down near the lunar south pole aboard either Starship or Blue Moon. (It's unclear at the moment which lander NASA will choose.)

NASA is currently targeting early 2028 for the launch of Artemis IV. If that schedule holds, the agency will beat China and pull off the first crewed lunar landing since Apollo 17 back in 1972.

But the new moon race won't end there, because this one isn't all about flags and footprints. Both NASA and China aim to build bases on the lunar surface over the next decade or so, setting up humanity's first true outpost on a world beyond Earth. The stakes are high, NASA and U.S. military officials have stressed: Whoever does so first can claim the best spots and get the best access to key lunar resources such as water ice. The leader will also get to establish norms of behavior on the moon, which at the moment is a bit of a Wild West of exploration.

#635. NASA reveals a haunting skull hidden in Antarctica’s ice

Located in the Weddell Sea, east of the Antarctic Peninsula, Vega Island has a particularly haunting appearance when viewed from above. Its rocky and icy features resemble a grinning skull seen from the side, seemingly gazing toward nearby Devil Island. But behind this unusual sight is a more serious story about the changing condition of Antarctica's glaciers.

NASA satellite images show the island during the beginning of Antarctic autumn and during spring. The images were captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard Landsat 9 on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.)

Several natural landmarks create the skull's distinctive appearance. A nunatak, which is a rocky peak rising above the surrounding ice, resembles an empty eye socket. A lateral moraine, a ridge of material left along the side of a glacier, outlines the mouth. Meanwhile, Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier forms what looks like the skull's lower jaw.

The two satellite views also reveal a striking difference in snow coverage. In March 2025, snow blanketed the icy terrain, consistent with March being the wettest month in the region. By October 2026, however, extensive sections of the island were free of snow, leaving darker glacier ice exposed.

Glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College explained that unusually warm conditions during the winter of 2026, especially in June, contributed to the unusually large areas of exposed ice observed in October. According to Pelto, the exposed surfaces on Vega Island and neighboring islands suggest that relatively little fresh snow accumulated over the winter. Some of that snow was also lost through sublimation, when ice turns directly into water vapor, and through strong winds that swept snow away.

“The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.”

The lack of snow could have important consequences as Antarctica moves into its warmer months. Fresh snow reflects much of the sunlight that reaches it, while darker, exposed ice absorbs more solar energy. As daylight increases and temperatures rise, these darker surfaces are likely to warm more quickly, potentially speeding up glacier melting.

Even a modest amount of new snowfall could temporarily slow that process by covering the exposed ice.

“Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” Pelto said.

Continued melting could also gradually transform the island's unsettling appearance. The same ice and rock formations that give Vega Island its skull shape are vulnerable to changes as the glaciers retreat.

“When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.”

Scientists have been studying Vega Island's glaciers for decades, and satellite observations have played an important role in documenting their condition.

One of the earliest detailed surveys appeared in a 1982 study that used early Landsat satellite data, aerial photography, and topographic maps to examine the island's ice cover. Researchers identified four ice caps, along with rocky cliffs extending above the ice and glaciers flowing outward from the ice caps. Altogether, they documented 29 glaciers across Vega Island.

One of these, Devil's Bay Glacier, has been monitored in detail since the Antarctic summer of 1998-1999. Measurements collected over that period show an overall reduction in the glacier's mass.

The changes are not limited to Devil's Bay Glacier. Satellite observations spanning recent decades reveal that other glaciers on Vega Island have also lost ice, exposing increasing amounts of the underlying bedrock.

Long before satellites began monitoring its ice, Vega Island played an unexpected role in one of Antarctica's dramatic early exploration stories.

The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901-1903 traveled to the region to investigate the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife of the eastern Antarctic Peninsula and surrounding areas. What began as a scientific mission turned into a desperate struggle for survival.

During the expedition, the explorers became separated into three groups, each forced to endure the Antarctic winter in a different location. Their situation became even more dangerous when pack ice destroyed their ship, leaving them stranded in one of the world's most unforgiving environments.

Despite the ordeal, Vega Island eventually became the setting for a moment of hope. In spring 1903, two of the separated groups reunited at a location later named Cape Well-met, near what now resembles the “forehead” of the island's giant skull.

Not long afterward, an Argentinean expedition arrived and rescued the survivors, bringing their extraordinary Antarctic ordeal to an end.

Today, Vega Island remains a place where dramatic natural formations, a remarkable history of exploration, and the effects of a changing climate come together. Its ghostly skull may be one of Antarctica's most unusual sights, but the gradual transformation of the ice that shapes it tells an even more important story.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey.

Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic

Eight years after touring with a combination of audience Q&As and solo music, Nick Cave will return to North America with “Conversations With Nick Cave: An Evening of Talk and Music,” a followup to his 2019 tour of the same name. This followup is set to run for 25 dates in the U.S. and Canada in the spring.

The shows begin April 9, 2027 at Vancouver’s Queen Elizabeth Theatre and wrap up May 21 at New Orleans’ Saenger Theatre. In the six weeks in-between, Cave has two-night stands booked at L.A.’s Orpheum (April 20-21), Brooklyn’s Kings Theatre (May 7-8) San Francisco’s Orpheum (April 16-17), Seattle’s 5th Ave. Theatre (April 13-14), Toronto’s Massey Hall (April 29-30) and Boston’s Boch Center Schubert Theatre (May 4-5). #633. Germany's search for a nuclear waste site

Finland has become the first country with a final storage facility for nuclear waste. Germany is still searching for a site, while some countries have yet to start. Costs are expected to total many billions of euros.

Hardly any environmental and political challenge is as complex as the disposal of radioactive waste from nuclear power plants. In almost all of the world's nuclear-powered nations — some 31 countries currently operate or once operated nuclear power plants — the issue remains largely unresolved. This is despite the first large-scale nuclear power plant going online 72 years ago in the Soviet Union.

Finland recently became the first country in the world to approve a repository for radioactive nuclear waste. Located 400 meters (1,300 feet) underground on an island in western Finland, it is situated at the site of one of the country's two nuclear power plants. The project took around 40 years to complete.

Yet in every other country, including Germany, the problem remains unresolved. To make an everyday analogy: The garbage has already been placed outside for collection, but the garbage truck has not yet arrived. There is simply no landfill to take it to. It is not a pleasant sight, yet hardly anyone wants to live near such a site.

Germany has made some progress: The specially established Federal Company for Radioactive Waste Disposal (BGE) has now been searching for a suitable site for almost ten years, one that, like the Finnish repository, would be located deep underground.

Most experts have long agreed on one point: Nuclear waste, especially the spent fuel elements from nuclear power plants, which will remain radioactive for many thousands of years, must be stored underground.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany hopes to identify a site for a final repository by 2050. But that is still a long way off, which is why Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) wants to examine whether the search process can be accelerated.

And, the government says, at least there is a roadmap in place. "Russia, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Japan have not yet advanced their procedures as far as we have," ministry spokesperson, Stephan Gabriel Haufe, said at a regular government press conference this week. "Finland is certainly the country making the fastest progress worldwide. But Germany is among the leading countries."

This week, the BGE announced that only 5% of Germany's land area, spread across 11 of the country's 16 states, remains under consideration as a potential site for a final repository. The agency is consulting geologists, nuclear experts, and physicists, as well as citizens and politicians. What is already clear, is that the nuclear waste generated during decades of nuclear power production will remain in Germany.

Most of the waste is currently stored at or near the sites where it was generated. These include the 19 former nuclear power plants currently being decommissioned, as well as several research facilities.

In 2011, following the reactor disaster in Fukushima, Japan, Germany decided to phase out the commercial use of nuclear energy, and the last nuclear power plant was shut down in 2023. The waste, however, remains in interim storage.

"It must be shown that a repository will remain safe over a very long period of time," said BGE spokesperson Dagmar Dehmer. "In Finland, that means 100,000 years; in Germany, Switzerland, and France, one million years. But no matter how far into the future scientists project, the effort involved is enormous. It requires a detailed analysis of developments over time, the interactions between geology and technology, and the decay of radionuclides, as well as an assessment of how these factors affect safety."

The procedure is indeed complex: First, potential sites are evaluated for their geological suitability. Will the rock formation remain stable at a depth of 400 meters? Could groundwater become contaminated? The goal is to identify a location where the repository would be surrounded by a rock layer around 100 meters thick, providing a natural barrier. Suitable geological formations include layers of clay, granite, and rock salt.

As the requirements become progressively stricter, fewer and fewer potential sites remain under consideration. Other factors, such as proximity to major cities, come into play only much later in the process. Few communities are likely to welcome a repository for radioactive waste, whether in an urban area or in the countryside.

Building and maintaining trust is also part of Dehmer's job. She often has to explain why it is important to deal with the legacy of the nuclear age, regardless of where people stand on nuclear energy.

Finland has succeeded in doing so, Dehmer believes. "There is a high level of trust in government action in Finland," she said. "The country's supervisory and licensing authority, STUK, is one of its most respected institutions. Germany can learn from Finland by remaining consistent, avoiding frequent changes in direction, and demonstrating the patience needed to achieve a successful outcome."

The disposal of nuclear waste is extremely expensive. Even today, the search for a final repository and the storage of nuclear waste at former reactor sites cost around €1.4 billion ($1.6 billion) per year.

Experts estimate that the final repository itself will cost roughly €14 billion ($16.4 billion) once completed. If all goes according to plan, 28,000 cubic meters of radioactive waste will eventually be stored deep underground on a permanent basis.

This article was originally published in German.

NASA has revealed a glimpse of its next X-plane, known as the X-70 Fractal.

Or at least what it thinks the X-70 will look like once built. The agency released a short statement on Wednesday (Nov. 4) announcing the X-plane, or experimental plane, declaring it to be a highly maneuverable test bed with a "rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology," allowing NASA to swap both external and internal components on-the-fly. This modular architecture will allow NASA to "explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight," according to the agency's statement.

The announcement was made alongside an AI-generated image showing two canted vertical tail fins emerging from swirling smoke. Little can be gleaned from the image about what final form the X-70 might take, but the tail fins are somewhat reminiscent of the Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor or Boeing F/A-18 Super Hornet.

"The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in the statement. The NASA chief called the aircraft "just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics" and said that the agency expects the X-70 to make its first flight within two years.

"This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly," Isaacman added.

NASA's statement fleshes out a few details about the X-70's capabilities. According to the agency, Fractal will fly at a cruise speed of Mach .75, about the same as a Boeing 737 Classic. The X-70 will be able to reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet (13.7 kilometers), and will have a range exceeding 1,726 miles (2,777 kilometers, or 1,500 nautical miles).

The X-70 Fractal will also be able to carry around 2,000 pounds (900 kg) of experimental payloads both internally and externally, which will allow for a "wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities," NASA said in the statement.

NASA adds it will have a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds (4,535 kilograms), around the same weight as the Scaled Composites- and Northrop Grumman-developed Model 437 Vanguard experimental aircraft. In fact, the two aircraft share a similar silhouette — at least in the AI image of the X-70 Fractal NASA has released so far.

The agency's most recent X-plane, the X-59, has been flying for over a year. That jet features a radical long-nosed geometry without a forward windscreen; pilots fly by way of an augmented reality screen that combines views from sensors and a forward-facing camera.

That geometry dampens the shockwaves coming off of the X-59 when it flies faster than the sound barrier, allowing it to fly at speeds over Mach 1 without the thunderous sonic booms that typically accompany supersonic flight.

There are numerous experimental aircraft being developed by private companies, such as Boom Supersonic's X-1 jet, which, like the X-59, aims to develop technologies that lessen the auditory impact of sonic booms on the ground.

In terms of other government X-plane projects, Boeing is working on the F-47, a next-generation stealth fighter for use by the U.S. military, and DARPA, the Pentagon's research agency, has an X-plane project of its own known as CRANE.

Brett is curious about emerging aerospace technologies, alternative launch concepts, military space developments and uncrewed aircraft systems. Brett's work has appeared on Scientific American, The War Zone, Popular Science, the History Channel, Science Discovery and more. Brett has degrees from Clemson University and the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. In his free time, Brett enjoys skywatching throughout the dark skies of the Appalachian mountains.

#631. A tiny squeeze dramatically changes the magnetism of exotic materials

Scientists at the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory have discovered that applying a small amount of pressure can dramatically alter the magnetic properties of a promising new class of materials called altermagnets. Using neutron experiments, the researchers uncovered how a simple mechanical squeeze can change the way these materials behave, offering a potential new approach to controlling magnetism.

The results, reported in two consecutive studies published in Physical Review X and Advanced Materials, show that mechanical strain can influence both magnetic structures and the movement of electrons. This ability could provide a straightforward way to control materials being investigated for advanced electronic technologies.

Why Altermagnets Matter for Future Electronics

One particularly promising application involves spintronics, short for spin electronics. Unlike conventional electronics, which processes and stores information using the electrical charge of electrons, spintronics also takes advantage of a property known as electron spin.

If scientists can identify and develop suitable materials, including altermagnets, this approach could lead to major advances in technologies ranging from wireless communication to quantum computing.

"By controlling the magnetic domains, we can directly influence the transport behavior, and that opens the door to exploring these materials for spintronic technologies," said Pengcheng Dai of Rice University, a former neutron scientist at ORNL.

A Simple Squeeze Reveals Surprising Magnetic Changes

To investigate how pressure affects these materials, the ORNL team placed tiny crystals of manganese telluride and iron sulfide between a pair of titanium plates and gently compressed them.

Using neutron diffraction at ORNL's Spallation Neutron Source, the scientists examined what happened to the magnetic structures inside the crystals. They found that the applied pressure changed the relative populations of magnetic domains, which are regions within a material that have particular magnetic arrangements. The strain also altered an electrical phenomenon called the anomalous Hall effect, providing evidence that the mechanical squeeze influenced the materials' electrical behavior.

"What's exciting is that one creative experimental idea -- a small mechanical squeeze between two plates -- can reveal entirely new magnetic behavior and push the field forward, and neutron scattering plays such a critical role, revealing the underlying change in magnetism," said Feng Ye, an ORNL neutron scientist and co-author on both linked publications.

The findings highlight how a relatively simple experiment can uncover new ways to manipulate magnetic materials, potentially helping researchers develop the building blocks for future spintronic devices.

ORNL's Spallation Neutron Source is a DOE Office of Science user facility.

When Jessica Watkins became commander of her mission to the International Space Station, she didn't just fulfill her duty as an astronaut — she made history.

Watkins is commanding SpaceX's Crew-13 mission, which launched her and three other astronauts to the International Space Station on Oct. 1. As their Crew Dragon capsule lifted off atop a Falcon 9 rocket that day, Watkins became the first Black woman to command a crewed mission to space. Spaceflight and space science are historically white and male-dominated fields, so this milestone carries incredible significance.

"This is certainly an important milestone, I think both for our agency and for the country," Watkins said in a press briefing ahead of Crew-13's launch.

This is Watkins' second spaceflight. She previously flew on SpaceX's Crew-4 mission in 2022 and has spent more than 200 days in space to date, though that number will keep climbing for a while, as Crew-13 is set to be an approximately six-month mission. A geologist, astronaut, aquanaut and former professional rugby player, Watkins brings an incredible variety of skills to her new role as mission commander. And, in addition to what she's bringing to her colleagues on mission, she's also providing some serious inspiration for those back on Earth.

"Jessica is an inspirational symbol to a lot of people," commercial astronaut and fellow geologist Sian Proctor, who became the first Black woman to pilot a spacecraft on SpaceX's private Inspiration4 mission to orbit in September 2021, told Space.com. Sian shared that the two even crossed paths years ago, when their astronaut training aligned.

"It just means so much to so many people when you see a diverse crew, and particularly women, and women of color, in leadership positions," Proctor said. "And it means something for America."

The visibility of Watkins' accomplishments and missions carries significant cultural weight. However, in addition to recognizing her many achievements, "you also should celebrate the fact that she's African American and a role model for her community," Proctor said.

Proctor, who similarly made spaceflight history with her mission, sees Watkins' role in Crew-13 as potentially more than just an exciting moment. Hopefully, she said, it will help lay the foundation for a more diverse future in human spaceflight.

"When they announced Jessica, I was super excited because it shows progress," Proctor said, sharing that she finds incredible importance in the "idea of looking at your crew and recognizing the fact that diversity makes the crew stronger."

While Watkins' historic milestone has been celebrated on social media and across the broader media landscape, NASA did not make a public statement commemorating the historic achievement. However, the agency confirmed its pioneering nature in an email to Space.com.

"NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins launched on her second spaceflight on Oct. 1, 2026, as commander of the agency's SpaceX Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station, becoming the first Black woman to command a crewed space mission," a NASA spokesperson wrote in the email.

"Watkins was selected as commander of Crew-13 based on her spaceflight experience, leadership, and ability to help the mission accomplish its objectives," the spokesperson added. "As a member of NASA's astronaut corps, she represents the best of America's talent, dedication, and spirit of exploration."

To date, the U.S. and the Soviet Union are the only nations to have launched Black astronauts into space. (The Soviets beat the U.S. to this milestone, launching Cuba's Arnaldo Tamayo Méndez in 1980. NASA's Guion Bluford became the first Black American in space three years later.) But, as Proctor shared, perhaps moments like this could serve to inspire other nations to follow suit.

"We can be a leader in saying, Look, if your country is diverse and has people from all different backgrounds, you should be encouraging them to apply and have a chance to be selected," Proctor said.

And, as a commercial astronaut herself, Proctor added that commercial space can continue to play a vital role in diversifying spaceflight.

"Jared did not even hesitate when he offered me the mission pilot seat for Inspiration4," Proctor said of her own selection as mission pilot by Jared Isaacman, the tech billionaire who funded and commanded the SpaceX mission. He now serves as NASA administrator.

"Commercial space has opened up so much opportunity and access. We are celebrating that because that's another way in which the space industry has diversified so much," Proctor added. "You can look at the history of space exploration and who's had access, and then you look at what commercial's done in the last five years, and it's incredible."

On the topic of the future of space exploration, Proctor expressed confidence that future crewed moon landings with NASA's Artemis program will be diverse.

"NASA is going to send diverse crews to the moon because they've done a good job of selecting diverse individuals with different heritages in their background," she said. NASA's current astronaut corps is roughly 45% women and 25% people of color. However, to-date only 6 Black women (including Watkins) have ever flown to space.

"Do I want to see more? Do I want women of color? Absolutely. They only have two Black women," Proctor said. But with the current diversity in NASA's astronaut corps as well as the continued development of commercial spaceflight, she is optimistic about a diverse future on the moon.

So far, NASA's Artemis program has been making some inroads when it comes to diversity. With Artemis II, we saw four people launch to the moon which included Victor Glover, the first person of color to ever travel beyond low-Earth orbit, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen who became the first woman and first non-American to make the same leap.

In reaching her own historic milestone as the first Black woman to pilot a spacecraft, Proctor understands that a historic moment like this carries not just incredible significance but a fair amount of personal pressure as well.

"If something goes wrong, because of who you are, maybe your gender or your ethnicity or race, you're looked at differently," she said. "When it goes right, you're not necessarily celebrated. But if it goes wrong, then that [adds to] that whole idea of 'not being qualified,'" that can come from prejudice.

"Because of who you are and the community you represent, you become the scapegoat," she added. "So, there's pressure to not have things go wrong and do everything you can to be better than the best."

But whether or not these pressures weigh on Watkins' mind, "we're all celebrating" back on Earth, Proctor said. "We're proud of her."

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. #629. Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response

Children who consume more ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may have stronger brain responses to tempting foods, potentially helping explain why these products are associated with weight gain. A new study published in JAMA Network Open found that children who ate more of these foods showed heightened activity in the brain's reward system when looking at pictures of appetizing foods. Those stronger responses were also associated with increases in body fat over the following year.

Ultra-processed foods include many everyday products, such as breakfast cereals, packaged bread, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and able to remain fresh for extended periods. Many contain artificial sweeteners, coloring agents, and other ingredients rarely used in home cooking. These products make up a substantial portion of children's diets, accounting for approximately 67% of the calories consumed by children in the United States.

Previous research has associated ultra-processed food consumption with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. However, scientists are still trying to understand the biological processes that might explain these connections. The new investigation, supported in part by the National Institutes of Health, combined magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), dietary assessments, and measurements of children's body composition to explore whether the brain's response to food could play a role.

"Children's brains are still developing, habits are still forming and food preferences are still being made. It's an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment," said the study's senior author, Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. "We're particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference."

Brain Scans Reveal a Link to Future Weight Gain

To investigate these connections, the research team studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the ongoing BrainChild study, which examines factors contributing to diabetes and obesity. Every participant had a healthy weight when the research began, giving scientists an opportunity to investigate potential warning signs before excess weight developed.

The brain scans revealed a notable pattern. Children who consumed larger amounts of ultra-processed foods showed greater activity in the dorsal striatum when viewing food pictures. This part of the brain helps regulate reward and motivation, making it particularly relevant to how people respond to desirable foods.

Importantly, children with stronger responses in this brain region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the next year. The findings suggest that heightened sensitivity to food cues may be one factor connecting ultra-processed diets with subsequent weight gain.

How Brain Reward Activity May Influence Body Fat

By the end of the study, children who consumed more ultra-processed foods generally had higher BMI, greater body fat percentage, and larger waist circumference.

The researchers then examined whether differences in brain activity could help account for these associations. When they adjusted their analysis to consider the children's responses in the dorsal striatum, the relationship between ultra-processed food intake and BMI became 31% weaker. The corresponding association with body fat percentage decreased by 44%.

These reductions suggest that the brain's reward response may help explain part of the relationship between ultra-processed food consumption and changes in body composition. Although the results do not demonstrate that these foods directly alter brain function, they provide a possible biological explanation for an association that has been observed in previous research.

"This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain," Page said. "It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time."

The researchers caution that improving children's diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed products are often inexpensive, widely available, and easy to prepare, making them practical choices for households facing financial or time constraints.

"Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution," Page said.

There are also important limitations to consider. Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether eating ultra-processed foods directly causes heightened brain activity or increases in body weight. The findings establish relationships between these factors, but additional research is needed to determine whether one causes another.

Page hopes to address that question in a future intervention study. The proposed research would provide children who regularly consume ultra-processed foods with more minimally processed alternatives. Scientists could then examine whether changing their diets affects how their brains respond to food images and whether any differences are associated with reduced weight gain.

Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue tracking participants as they move through puberty and into early adulthood. By monitoring brain development, body composition, dietary patterns, and general health over time, researchers hope to gain a clearer picture of how childhood nutrition may influence long-term health.

The study was led by Page alongside Jasmin M. Alves, Ella Morgan, Brendan Angelo, Kianna Le, and Jared Smith from the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes, Department of Medicine, and Diabetes and Obesity Research Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California. Additional contributors included Kay Jann of the USC Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California, and Ting Chow and Anny H. Xiang of the Department of Research and Evaluation at Kaiser Permanente Southern California in Pasadena, California.

Spacewalks are hard work, so sometimes you need to take a break for a moment and snap a gorgeous selfie with your home planet in the background.

During a pre-Halloween spacewalk on Oct. 29, 2026, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk took a moment to pose for a photograph.

In this moment, the International Space Station to which he was tethered was orbiting 267 miles (430 kilometers) above the South Atlantic Ocean down below on Earth.

During this spacewalk — the first for a Canadian since 2019 — Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon worked together to install a new roll-out solar array on the station while also performing some "get ahead" tasks to prep for the next spacewalk, which is happening today (Nov. 5).

During today's excursion, the same two astronauts will venture out into space, tethered to the space station, to install the eighth and final roll-out solar array. These eight new arrays will boost the station's available power by a total of 30%, according to NASA officials.

When we think of astronauts working in space, we might think of the important science and research they're doing aboard the station. Astronauts work on everything from biomedical research to plant science and physics experiments. But the job also includes work on the space station itself.

Sometimes they have to venture out into the vacuum of space to fix urgent problems. These situations can be tense, and there's a lot of pressure to get things absolutely right.

But even spacewalks that do relatively mundane maintenance work, like the one on Oct. 29, come with pressure. Every minute that astronauts spend outside of the space station, there are countless risk factors floating around. Earth orbit is a very harsh environment, after all, even if it does allow for some pretty amazing selfies.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. #627. Ethnic Germans in Kazakhstan face legacy of the Soviet Union

Kazakhstan is struggling to deal with the legacy of the Soviet dictatorship. Some 85 years ago, Stalin deported hundreds of thousands of people: Some 400,000 ethnic Germans living in the USSR were sent to Kazakhstan.

She wants to keep history alive. Yunna Kinereish, 22, is studying public relations in Kazakhstan's modern capital, Astana. She describes herself as a Kazakh German.

"I am German by ethnicity. But I also feel that I'm Kazakh, because I keep the traditions with my family, and I have this mentality," she told DW.

Kinereish, who belongs to the Wiedergeburt (Revival) Association of Germans in Kazakhstan, is one of 223,000 Kazakh Germans living in the Central Asian republic of Kazakhstan today.

Kinereish recently acted in a play at the association's youth theater that told the fate of her Russian German forebears.

From the 18th century onward, Germans were incentivized to leave Germany and settle in the Russian empire, including in Ukraine's Black Sea region.

But after the armies of Hitler's Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941, Soviet dictator Josef Stalin started deporting hundreds of thousands of Germans living in Russia and Ukraine to Siberia and Kazakhstan.

Innocent people who had nothing to do with Nazi Germany's invasion and atrocities were collectively held responsible by the Soviet power and denounced as spies and collaborators.

There were more than a million deportees, of whom at least 200,000 died as a result of expulsion, hunger, and forced labor.

"My family is part of this history, these terrible times. They were driven out of the Ukrainian village Kleinwärter, a settlement of ethnic Germans in Ukraine."

Yunna Kinereish says she was very moved by the personal stories she and her friends had brought to the stage at the House of Friendship, where the association has its office. "It's not easy for me, because it all touches my heart very deeply. I actually feel like crying. But when I'm on stage ..., I have to be strong."

The modern-looking House of Friendship in the capital Astana is the center for German culture in the city. Financed primarily by the German government, it offers language courses, engages in social work and fosters a culture of remembrance, focusing on the themes of deportation and repression under the Soviet regime.

Yunna Kinereish doesn't only present the history of her people on stage: She is also documenting it on film. In 2025, she made a film about German women incarcerated in ALZhIR (Akmolinsk Camp for Wives of Traitors to the Motherland), among the most infamous in the Soviet Gulag system.

During Stalin's brutal campaign of political repression and state-sponsored terror in the 1930s, a period known as the Great Terror, the Soviet Union established its biggest camp system in Kazakhstan. 18,000 women passed through the ALZhIR camp alone. These women were imprisoned there only because their husbands had been convicted of being traitors or enemies of the people. Among them were 167 ethnic German women, whose stories are told in the film.

The memorial for the ALZhIR women's camp is located just outside the gates of Astana, which only became the capital in 1997.

Astana's roads are permanently clogged with traffic. There are almost no pedestrians, and no cyclists at all. The city is growing, with new buildings shooting up all along the outskirts of the city. Beyond them is the barren steppe; the village of Akmol is about an hour's drive away.

Before entering the actual ALZhIR museum, the visitor passes through the Arch of Grief, a huge steel construction that commemorates the suffering and forced labor the women endured. The museum itself contains personal items that belonged to the female prisoners, models of their primitive quarters, original documents and photographs.

One of the photos is of Gertrud Platais, a woman with German roots who spent years incarcerated in ALZhIR. Platais was a print worker from Lower Silesia, part of modern-day Poland. She married Karl Eduard Platais and became a Soviet citizen. In 1938, during the Great Terror, her husband was arrested. Gertrud was convicted, too as a "relative of a traitor to the homeland."

She was transferred to ALZhIR, in a region where temperatures hit 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer and minus 40 degreees Celsius in winter. Here, she was forced to work as an embroiderer until 1946. After this, she was banished for life to the huge Karaganda Corrective Labor Camp, known as Karlag. Gertrud Platais wasn't rehabilitated until 1956. Hers is just one story documenting the terror of the Soviet system on Kazakh soil.

Karlag was by far the biggest camp system, and its complex covered an area about 22 times the size of New York City. Karlag was not just a prison camp, but a huge economic and agricultural complex. Almost one million people passed through it between 1931 and 1959.

Around 10,000 prisoners are believed to have died here between 1940 and 1950 alone: of starvation, cold, sickness, and the effects of forced labor.

The museum sits in the middle of the Kazakh steppe, near the city of Karaganda, about 250 kilometers south of Astana. It is located in the building that used to house the camp system administration. Visiting German historians and specialists are slightly puzzled: People were not tortured or tormented in this building, it was simply where the administration was done.

Here, interrogation and torture cells have been reconstructed, and everything is underscored by melodramatic music pouring from ubiquitous loudspeakers. It comes across as staged rather than authentic. As at the ALZhIR memorial, the Karlag museum has few visitors. Even well-educated young Kazakhs probably don't know about it."

Many people in Kazakhstan, and certain areas of politics, have almost no interest in coming to terms with the country's often brutal history," says Katherine M. Erdman. An American anthropologist and archaeologist at the Nazarbayev University in Astana, she has been researching the Gulag system for about a decade now.

"We wanted to find out where exactly the camps were, and how they can still be recognized today." Erdman and her students relied on modern technology such as drone flights, but conducting interviews and research on the ground was also a part of it.

"In many regions, the landscape has been shaped by forced labor," Erdman says. Factories were often constructed alongside the primitive living quarters. Houses were built using bricks made by forced laborers.

The researchers share their findings directly with neighbors and with local administrations. "Often we're just met with apathy, or flat-out rejection," says Erdman. At a time of economic and social advancement, many don't want to be reminded of the inglorious aspects of the past.

Erdman says there is a desire to demonstrate to the international community that the country is dealing with the dark side of its history, but that she often experiences lack of interest and even rejection. The academic has been conducting research in Kazakhstan for a decade, but there is no state funding for a further lectureship.

The Kazakh German Yunna Kinereish is one of the young people in Kazakhstan who want to ensure that the past is not forgotten. "My ancestors survived the Gulag system in Kazakhstan," she tells DW. "So it's important to me that we don't forget our roots, and that what our forefathers experienced and suffered is passed on."

This article, originally published in German, was written in the context of a study trip organized by the Federal Foundation for the Study of the Communist Dictatorship in Germany. Since 1998, the foundation, funded by the German taxpayer, has dedicated itself to studying and reappraising the former communist dictatorships in Germany, the GDR, and other countries.

#626. Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them

Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative way to turn a chemical produced by cancer cells into a weapon against them. Instead of delivering toxic drugs throughout the body, their experimental approach uses carbon monoxide released by cancer cells to manufacture anticancer compounds directly inside the cells themselves.

The research, led by Katsunori Tanaka at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI) in Japan, was published in Nature Communications. In laboratory experiments, the team demonstrated that a specially designed compound could trigger drug production inside cancer cells without generating the same toxic substances in healthy cells. Although the technique is still at an early stage, it could eventually provide a way to attack tumors while reducing the harmful side effects associated with conventional cancer treatments.

Turning Cancer's Own Toxic Gas Against It

One of the greatest challenges in cancer treatment is destroying malignant cells without damaging healthy tissue. Traditional chemotherapy can cause serious side effects because its toxic effects are not always limited to tumors. Tanaka and other researchers are investigating more selective strategies that could make cancer treatments safer.

Their long-term goal is to replace the direct delivery of toxic drugs with relatively harmless compounds that become active only after entering cancer cells. These compounds would use substances already present inside tumors to generate therapeutic drugs exactly where they are needed.

Carbon monoxide offers an intriguing opportunity for this approach. Although best known as a poisonous gas produced by sources such as gasoline engines, carbon monoxide is also generated naturally by many types of cancer cells. Because tumors can produce unusually high amounts of the gas, it may serve as a useful biological marker for identifying cancer cells, provided it can be detected.

Scientists in RIKEN's Biofunctional Synthetic Chemistry Laboratory investigated whether they could exploit this difference. Their strategy involved delivering a metal catalyst into cells and using the excess carbon monoxide in cancer cells to drive a chemical reaction that produces a toxic compound. In principle, the reaction would occur primarily in cancer cells, where enough carbon monoxide is available, while sparing normal cells.

Protecting the Catalyst Inside Cancer Cells

To make the system work, the researchers turned to a class of compounds known as palladacycles. These metal-containing compounds can react with carbon monoxide to produce an organic molecule called phenanthridinone. Certain derivatives of phenanthridinone are toxic to cells and have already been incorporated into anticancer drugs.

However, there was a major obstacle. When palladacycles are introduced directly into cells, substances such as glutathione rapidly deactivate their central palladium catalyst. Without an active catalyst, the reaction cannot produce the desired drug.

Tanaka's team addressed this problem by building on its previous work using metal catalysts to carry out chemical reactions in living systems. The researchers enclosed a palladacycle within albumin, a protein commonly found in blood. This protective protein carrier allows the complex to travel through the bloodstream while shielding the palladium catalyst from substances that would otherwise deactivate it after entering cells.

Laboratory Tests Reveal Selective Drug Production

The scientists evaluated their system through a series of experiments. They began by testing different palladacycles to identify which one could generate the greatest amount of phenanthridinone.

Next, they exposed cultured human liver, cervical, breast, and lung cancer cells to the albumin and palladacycle complex for 48 hours. They also tested the compound on a noncancerous cell line to determine whether the same chemical reaction would occur in healthy cells.

After 48 hours, the researchers detected phenanthridinone in the cancer cell lines but not in the normal cells. The findings indicated that the albumin carrier successfully protected the catalyst from glutathione and that the chemical reaction occurred selectively in the cancer cells under the conditions tested.

The team then refined the system so that the newly formed compound could separate from the carrier and move freely throughout the cell. Additional modifications allowed the reaction to generate a particularly toxic phenanthridinone derivative already used in anticancer drugs.

When the researchers introduced this modified system into cultured liver cancer cells, they observed the anticancer compound forming inside the cells. The cells subsequently showed signs of damage caused by the toxic drug, providing proof that the approach could generate a cancer-fighting substance directly within its intended target.

Why the Experimental Drug Did Not Form in Blood

An important safety concern involved carbon monoxide already present in the bloodstream. If that gas triggered the chemical reaction before the compound reached cancer cells, the resulting drug could damage blood cells instead of its intended target.

Fortunately, laboratory testing showed that the toxic drug was not produced in blood. The researchers believe this is because carbon monoxide in the bloodstream is largely attached to hemoglobin, the protein responsible for transporting oxygen. In this bound form, the gas appears to be unavailable for the reaction needed to manufacture the drug.

The finding suggests that the system may be able to travel through blood without prematurely generating harmful substances, although further studies will be needed to establish its safety in living organisms.

"This work represents an important advance in therapeutic in vivo synthetic chemistry," says Tanaka. "In our therapeutic strategy, molecules naturally present or generated within the body -- including disease-associated metabolites -- are used as endogenous chemical feedstocks to synthesize therapeutic molecules directly at the site of disease."

The researchers now plan to move beyond cultured cells and test the approach in animal models. If future experiments are successful, the technology could help establish a new class of cancer treatments that exploit the chemistry of tumors to produce drugs directly at the disease site, potentially limiting damage to healthy tissue.

#625. Merck tops quarterly estimates, hikes profit outlook as new Keytruda form shows strength

Merck on Thursday topped third-quarter estimates and hiked its adjusted profit outlook, as its immunotherapy Keytruda, including a newer injectable form of the drug, showed stronger-than-expected sales.

The pharmaceutical giant now expects adjusted earnings to be between $2.77 and $2.82 per share. That adjusted profit outlook is up from a previous range of $2.66 to $2.76 per share. The guidance now includes a one-time charge of $400 million, or 12 cents per share, related to its licensing agreement with the Chinese cancer drugmaker SciBrunch.

Merck also narrowed the low end of its 2026 revenue guidance, now expecting sales between $66.8 billion and $67.3 billion. That compares to a previous outlook of $66.3 billion to $67.3 billion.

The company has been on a deal spree as it races to offset generic competition for Keytruda after key patents begin expiring in 2028.

Merck is also positioning the new form of the drug, Keytruda Qlex, as a cornerstone of its growth strategy. The goal is to transition patients from the original intravenous version to Qlex, considered a more convenient under-the-skin injection. This strategy allows the company to defend its market share and sustain Keytruda's blockbuster sales beyond the original version's loss of exclusivity.

Keytruda raked in $8.60 billion in sales for the quarter, beating the $7.73 billion that analysts were expecting, according to StreetAccount. That includes $830 million in sales for Qlex – the highest seen in a quarter since it launched in 2025.

Analysts were expecting $649 million in sales, StreetAccount estimates said. The blowout quarter for the shot suggests it could soon eventually be a multibillion-dollar product annually.

Here's what Merck reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

The company posted a net income of $5.07 billion, or $2.04 per share, for the quarter. That compares with net income of $5.79 billion, or $2.32 per share, for the year-earlier period.

Excluding acquisition and restructuring costs, Merck posted earnings of $2.49 per share for the third quarter.

Merck raked in $18.09 billion in revenue for the quarter, up 5% from the same period a year earlier.

Beyond Keytruda, Merck's newer products also showed strong growth.

Winrevair, which is used to treat a rare, deadly lung condition, generated $694 million in sales for the quarter, up 93% from the same period a year earlier. Analysts were expecting sales of $645 million.

Meanwhile, the Gardasil vaccine, which prevents cancers from HPV, a very common sexually transmitted infection, drew about $2 billion in sales due to higher demand in the U.S. That tops the $1.76 billion in sales that analysts were expecting.

That strong revenue comes after Merck last year grappled with elevated Gardasil inventory and weak demand for the vaccine in China.

Meanwhile, Merck's animal health business posted $1.68 billion in sales for the third quarter, which came in slightly below analysts' estimates.
